title: E-means: Outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs
body_text: e-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss - Blog Swann Bessa Blog post Playground Video Paper On arXiv: arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501 @misc{bessa2026emeansoutperformingkmeansin, title={e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)}, author={Swann Bessa and Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré and Gergely Szilvasy and Hugo Touvron and David Picard and Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou}, year={2026}, eprint={2611.09501}, archivePrefix={arXiv}, primaryClass={cs.LG}, url={https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09501}, } Copy citation Open on arXiv Code e-means is available in faiss : faiss/contrib/e_means e-means: outperforming k-means in one-tenth the epochs I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss. Try e-means in your browser [Paper] · [Code] · [Cite] · [Coauthors] Pierre-Emmanuel Mazaré, Gergely Szilvasy, Hugo Touvron, David Picard, Matthijs Douze and Hervé Jégou Lloyd (full batch) e-means (batch and step from the scaling laws) Training MSE e-means Lloyd ▶︎ epochs: 0.0 100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means. An order of magnitude less epochs Across a large range of scales and datasets , e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans [2] ), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss [1] . Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss. The k-means problem Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x 1 , ..., x n } ⊂ R d and an integer k , the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c 1 , ..., c k ) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid: \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2, \qquad a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] \[ \mathrm{MSE}(X, C) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \|x_i - c_{a(i)}\|^2 \] \[ a(i) = \arg\min_{j \in \{1,\dots,k\}} \|x_i - c_j\|^2 \] It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving. The e-means project The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations: k-means is one of the rare problems in machine learning where full-batch optimization is still widely used. Mini-batch k-means methods in the literature exist [3] , [4] , [5] , but are mostly based on the MacQueen update rule, released in 1967. Modern deep learning offers optimization tools that can enhance mini-batch methods. For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages [6] , which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws ). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups. Moving-average updates Each mini-batch updates every cluster's count and sum. The centroid is their ratio. old centroid new centroid batch mean No hyperparameter tuning Everything is derived from scaling laws. log n, log k, log T Start and finish Novel initialization and finalization methods. The run ends on each cluster's exact last-epoch mean. start exact mean Cosine scheduling The step α anneals from α 0 to 0.1 α 0 , as a learning rate does. α₀ 0.1 α₀ Dead-cluster revival Clusters with size below a threshold are revived by splitting a large cluster. below threshold large cluster split in two Specialized kernels GPU kernels fuse the nearest-centroid assignment, turning the epoch savings above into matching wall-clock speedups. naive PyTorch fused kernel The centroid update rules The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j , a sum S j and a count N j of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio: \[ c_j = S_j / N_j \] They differ only in how S j and N j are updated. Below, s j and n j denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are). Lloyd’s algorithm [7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch: \[ S_j \leftarrow s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow n_j \] so c j is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations). MacQueen’s update [3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them: \[ S_j \leftarrow S_j + s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow N_j + n_j \] so c j is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means [8] , a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters. e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average: \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j, \qquad\quad N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] \[ S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j \] \[ N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \] so older assignments are forgotten at rate α , and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs [6] . What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned. Why exponential moving average updates and not gradient descent? The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull. Test error against the effective step a centroid takes, at a large batch, for exponential-moving-average updates (EMA) and plain gradient descent (SGD), each at every step setting tried. DEEP, 1 million vectors, and SIFT, 10 million vectors, 16,384 clusters, 5 epochs, median over 3 seeds. The vertical axis is percent above the best test error in the panel. At its best setting, gradient descent ends 1.6% (DEEP) and 0.4% (SIFT) above the moving average. In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method. Lloyd is a special case of e-means: hyperparameter study If you set the batch to the full dataset, B  =  n , and α  = 1, then N j and S j become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α : Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest. Validation loss for every batch B and step α , relative to the best cell, after 5 epochs. DEEP, n  = 10 6 , k  = 1024. The step is constant here (no cosine schedule) so that Lloyd is exactly one of the cells: full batch, α  = 1. The lowest losses follow a diagonal band, a larger batch calls for a larger step. This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α . e-means better escapes local minima To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Two blobs of very different sizes, k  = 8. Lloyd puts two centroids on the small blob and leaves the large one short. e-means starts in the same trap and leaves it within its first epochs, ending with seven centroids on the large blob and one on the small. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 26% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 3.5% of times. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Nine blobs in a 3×3 grid with heavier corners, k  = 10. Lloyd leaves the centre blob without a centroid and crowds three into a corner. e-means falls into the same arrangement, then climbs out around epoch 10. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck more than 1% worse on 43% of starts, while e-means is more than 1% worse on 4%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Four blobs on a square around a heavier centre blob, k  = 5. Lloyd puts two centroids on one corner blob and strands one in the gap between two others, which then share it. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 15.5% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Lloyd (full batch) e-means (mini-batches of 256) ▶︎ training MSE Five blobs on a line, k  = 5. Lloyd leaves a light middle blob without a centroid and gives an end blob two. e-means, from the same start, gives every blob one. Over 200 starts Lloyd stays stuck on 46% of starts, while e-means stays stuck on 0%. Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them. Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α 0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T) , and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales. \[ B = c_B \, k^{b_k} \, n^{b_n} \, T^{b_T} \] \[ \alpha_0 = \min\!\Big(c_\alpha \, k^{a_k} \, B^{a_B} \, n^{a_n} \, T^{a_T},\; 1\Big) \] law constant exponent of regret, held-out datasets regret, held-out size R² k B n T step α 0 0.824 −0.46 0.90 −0.45 −0.11 0.07% 0.07% 0.95 batch B , default 0.035 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.19% 0.20% 0.96 batch B , quality law 0.0044 0.13 n/a 0.88 0.81 0.07% 0.06% n/a Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE [9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted. We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α 0 (left) and batch size B (right). The importance of dead-cluster revival Revival off dead clusters: 0 of 25 Revival on (e-means) dead clusters: 0 of 25 centroid dead cluster (no points) cluster boundaries ▶︎ epochs: 0.00 · update 0 of 157 Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival. The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today. A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec [10] , where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity. dataset revival policy dead clusters of codebook imbalance test MSE DEEP proportional split 47 0.3% 1.194 0.38762 resample from batch (EnCodec) 2,343 14.3% 1.423 0.39124 off 4,313 26.3% 1.647 0.39448 SIFT proportional split 10 0.1% 1.186 0.19623 resample from batch (EnCodec) 750 4.6% 1.233 0.19684 off 2,080 12.7% 1.404 0.19797 1 million vectors, k  = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper ’s revival ablation table. Extensive experimental validation We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper ). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map . Train (top) and test (bottom) MSE, divided by Lloyd’s after 25 epochs. Initialized from random vectors. Test MSE against wall-clock time on one H100, 10 million vectors, 65,536 clusters. 25 epochs of a plain PyTorch Lloyd (data on the GPU, bf16) take 142 to 155 seconds, against 14 to 22 seconds for Flash-KMeans [2] . Labels on the curves mark the number of epochs. Epochs e-means needs to reach the test error Lloyd reaches in 25 epochs, on the 11 datasets of the VIBE embedding benchmark (text, code, image and multimodal embeddings, d  = 200 to 3,072, k  = 8,192 or 16,384). Budgets spaced 0.2 epochs apart, median over five seeds. Every dataset needs between 1.6 and 2.4 epochs, against Lloyd’s 25. title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
body_text: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 \ Anthropic Skip to main content News Research Policy Commitments Company Try Claude Introduction Performance and efficiency Coding Cybersecurity Science and engineering Safety and alignment Data privacy Availability November 9, 2026 Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 [1] Introduction [2] Performance and efficiency [3] Science and engineering [4] Safety and alignment [5] Availability We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below. Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens. Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks. We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card . When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models). Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 Benchmark performance. Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested. Theoretical physics Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics. Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here . Protein folding Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid , can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together. Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies: Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Dyno Therapeutics Columbia University Biohub Quote “This acceleration could save meaningful time and cost from our capsid folding pipeline, enabling us to deploy compute more efficiently across many capsid properties that are needed for a genetic medicine. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas. Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem , performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30. Alignment testing We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences). We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1. The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss. Safeguards Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas. AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators. Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report , which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%. We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features). Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards , automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). title: Payments Canada announces launch of Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system
body_text: Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy | Payments Canada Skip to main content A new source of strength for Canada’s economy: Canada's Real-Time Rail (RTR) is now live. Learn more × Canada's Real-Time Rail is here Top Contact Careers Subscribe Search Français Payments Canada Systems & services Main Navigation Payment systems Real-Time Rail payment system Retail batch payment system High-value payment system - Lynx Payments Canada fees System closure schedule Payment services Payment file validation service Message validation service Financial institutions file Corporate creditor identification number database APIs Rules & documentation Payment resources Main Navigation Directories Support guides Consumer guides Business guides Financial institution guides Cheque printer guide ISO 20022 Automatic funds transfer High-value payment system - Lynx Real-Time Rail payment system Glossary Education Insights Main Navigation News & research Corporate reports Modernization Connect Main Navigation Careers Annual conference Events Membership Payment service provider participation Contact About Main Navigation Who we are Our members & stakeholders Members Stakeholders Our leadership Governance & risk Board of directors Legislation & by-laws Risk management Menu Menu Home Insights News & research Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy News Canada launches the Real-Time Rail, bringing 24/7 payment infrastructure to the national economy November 9, 2026 The new system will enable participating financial service providers to clear and settle payments in real time, providing a made-in-Canada platform for future innovation and prosperity. OTTAWA, ON, November 9, 2026 – Payments Canada today announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR). This new national payment system will transform day-to-day payments for Canadian businesses and consumers by enabling instant speed and settlement, real-time cash-flow visibility and data-rich messaging through existing banking and payment channels. The launch of Canada’s RTR marks a major milestone in modernizing the critical infrastructure that underpins Canada’s economy and future growth. The RTR will enable participating members, including financial institutions, credit unions and payment service providers, to exchange, clear and settle payments securely in real time for their customers, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. “A stronger, more productive economy relies on modern financial infrastructure that can match our ambition,” said the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne, Minister of Finance and National Revenue. “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail lays the foundation for a more dynamic and competitive digital economy, driving innovation, expanding choice and creating new opportunities for Canadians while positioning our country for long-term growth.” “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail marks the beginning of a new era for payments in our country,” said Susan E. Hawkins , President and CEO, Payments Canada. “As a national asset that’s designed specifically for our country, the RTR gives the payment ecosystem a modern foundation to build on. By collectively leveraging this rail, our ecosystem will unleash its full potential, enabling our members to build capabilities that drive innovation, resilience and growth for businesses and consumers across the nation.” Image Ron Morrow, the Honourable François-Philippe Champagne and Susan E. Hawkins The RTR will drive significant cost savings and economic growth in Canada over the next decade. The C.D. Howe Institute projects that, with its functionalities at launch, the RTR will generate up to $14.5 billion in cost savings from lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient). Extending beyond these cost savings, the RTR is expected to generate $16 billion in economic gains , growing to $27 billion as new functionalities are introduced over time. “The Real-Time Rail is an important step in modernizing Canada's payment infrastructure and ensuring it keeps pace with Canadians' evolving needs,” said Tiff Macklem, Governor of the Bank of Canada. “The Bank will oversee the system so that it operates safely and reliably while ensuring Canadians can benefit from innovations in financial services.” Owned and operated by Payments Canada, and built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac Corp., the RTR leverages ISO 20022 data-rich messaging. Through this shared technical language, the RTR holds the potential to strengthen Canada’s economic sovereign autonomy and support its global competitiveness. Fraud safeguards from day one Canada is the first G7 country to deploy a real-time payment system with mandatory centralized fraud services for use at launch. These services will be used alongside participants’ existing fraud controls to mitigate the risk of fraud for Canadian businesses and consumers at multiple levels. Fraud controls required at the launch of Canada’s RTR include: Confirmation of payee (available for consumer accounts on day one) A fraud transaction “safety” score A risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators A fraud reporting and intelligence platform While no system is entirely immune to risk, these measures establish a strong, coordinated layer of defence across the payment network. At-launch member participants The initial cohort of active RTR system participants includes: Wealthsimple Questbank Peoples Trust Company Paramount Commerce KOHO DoBusiness.com™ Digital Commerce Bank Bank of America Canada’s deliberately sequenced RTR rollout pairs day-one security with rapid scalability. With additional participants onboarding continually in the coming months, including all major Canadian financial institutions and other members applying for access, the RTR will be available to more than nine in 10 Canadians within the first year after launch. Made-in Canada, for Canada The launch of the RTR reflects our ‘Team Canada’ approach, bringing together regulators, members, stakeholders and delivery partners around a shared vision . Built in Canada and designed to serve all Canadians, the RTR provides accessible payment infrastructure through existing banking and payment channels. This infrastructure supports a diverse country and a broad range of communities, including small businesses, newcomers and people in rural areas.  Payments Canada research found that 60 per cent of Canadian businesses are ready to adopt real-time payments to address everyday challenges such as forecasting cash flow and waiting to send and receive funds. More than half of surveyed consumers (52 per cent) also expressed interest and intent to use real-time payments. To meet this evolving need, the RTR serves as a secure platform for innovation. With it, system participants can build and offer products and services that benefit consumers and businesses across the country, supporting a changing economy and Canada's future prosperity. An infrastructure for the future Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important step toward a more productive, innovative and inclusive economy, and the work will continue to ensure the country’s payment infrastructure meets Canadians’ evolving needs. Learn more about Canada’s Real-Time Rail Contributed quotes At-launch member participants "When Canada embraces new technology, innovation and competition follow, and consumers benefit. Canadians deserve instant, seamless, low-cost financial products to power their businesses and their lives. The Real-Time Rail can transform how money moves in this country, with payments that arrive in seconds instead of days. We’re proud to be among the first institutions to join the RTR and bring this technology to the millions of Canadians who trust us with their money." Mike Katchen, CEO and Co-Founder Wealthsimple "Canadians deserve a modern financial system that operates at the speed of everyday life. The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a pivotal turning point—it puts individuals in direct, immediate control of their money around the clock. We are proud to join Payments Canada in unlocking a safer, more dynamic financial ecosystem for everyone across the country." Rob Galaski, President Questrade Financial Group (Questbank) "The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a transformative milestone for Canada’s financial ecosystem. As a proud member of Payments Canada and a settlement agent at launch, Peoples Group is pleased to support the foundational clearing and settlement that brings real-time payments to life. We are committed to supporting innovative businesses across the country, and look forward to direct participation as the rail expands to serve even more Canadians." David Raju, President and CEO Peoples Group "Being first-to-market on the Real-Time Rail lets our merchants and partners benefit immediately from 24/7 settlement, higher transaction limits and proactive fraud defence. As one of Payments Canada's first payment service provider (PSP) members, we’re proud to have worked alongside their team to help advance Canada’s payment infrastructure and support the next chapter of payments innovation." Sereena Boparai, Chief Revenue Officer Paramount Commerce "The Real-Time Rail is a significant step forward for the integrity and resilience of Canada's payment infrastructure. Building payment systems that are instant, secure and always on takes real rigour, and it's the kind of foundation a modern financial system depends on. We're excited to be part of this work with Payments Canada, and to help ensure Canadians benefit from payment infrastructure built to the highest standards.” David Merriby, CEO The future KOHO Bank “DoBusiness.com™ is honoured to be one of the very first participants on Canada’s Real-Time Rail. The RTR's launch represents a milestone in how money moves across Canada and its payments sovereignty. For us, faster payments and superior fraud prevention belong together. This is an opportunity for us to help Canadian businesses modernize how they pay and verify account details before money moves.” Shayle Rothman, CEO and Co-Founder DoBusiness.com™ “We’re proud to be part of the Team Canada effort that brought the Real-Time Rail to life. For years we’ve helped fintechs and other corporate clients build and launch the payment services Canadians use every day. With the RTR, those companies can now give their customers faster, more robust ways to move money, right from launch.” Jeff Smith, CEO DCBank "The Real-Time Rail is an important investment in Canada's economic future. Instant, data-rich payments will give Canadian businesses and their trading partners more visibility and control over their cash, and we look forward to bringing those benefits to our clients.” Lyndsay Langford, Head of Global Payments Solutions for Canada Bank of America Delivery partners “Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone and a powerful example of what national collaboration can achieve. More than a modernization of payments, it represents an investment in critical infrastructure that will support Canada’s digital economy for generations to come. CGI is proud to have contributed alongside Payments Canada, Interac and our fellow delivery partners to this made-in-Canada initiative. Together, we’re laying the foundation for faster, more secure and resilient payments, opening new opportunities for businesses, financial institutions and Canadians. Through this work, we’re helping build what’s next for Canada’s digital economy.” Michael Godin, President, Canada Operations CGI “Deloitte is very proud to have supported Payments Canada and its members deliver the technical solution for the Real-Time Rail project. This ‘made-in-Canada’ initiative will be a critical foundation for innovation and productivity in Canada while better protecting Canadians against financial crimes. We look forward to welcoming new members to the RTR and continued collaboration for the benefit of Canadians.” Todd Roberts, Global Payments Leader Deloitte Canada “Canadians expect payments to be fast and easy, but behind that experience, the infrastructure has to be secure, resilient and built for the future. Building a real-time payment system at this scale takes deep payments and technology experience, relentless testing and close collaboration. As the technology implementation partner, IBM Canada has worked alongside Payments Canada and its partners to bring that experience to the Real-Time Rail, helping build a strong foundation for the next generation of payments and innovation in Canada.” Matthew Wetmore, Managing Partner and Market Leader, Consulting IBM Canada “As the RTR’s Technical Operator and first Fraud Services Provider, Interac is proud to support Payments Canada and the wider payment ecosystem in achieving this historic launch milestone. We bring more than 40 years of experience to these roles, and our commitment is clear: to operate always-on infrastructure Canadians can trust. As Interac e-Transfer payments begin to clear and settle on the RTR, we will put this world-class infrastructure to work for consumers and businesses.” Jeremy Wilmot, President and CEO Interac Corp. Payments Canada Member and Stakeholder Advisory Councils “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone for Canada’s payment ecosystem and reflects the sustained commitment and collective effort of members in bringing it to launch. The RTR establishes a modern, made-in-Canada foundation for real-time, data-rich payments that will support innovation, efficiency and improved payment experiences. As members build on this foundation, the focus will be on delivering new capabilities and experiences that create real value for consumers and businesses across Canada." Michael Liberty Vice President, Global Money Operations, CIBC Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Chair “The launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail is an important milestone for the stakeholder community and for the future of payments in Canada. By creating greater access to real-time payment infrastructure, the RTR opens new opportunities for stakeholders across the ecosystem to participate, innovate and compete. The RTR is a platform that enables new ideas, products and services that can deliver more seamless payment experiences for Canadians, and on behalf of the Stakeholder Advisory Council, we look forward to seeing what new possibilities this creates for payments in Canada.” Daniela Aubry Chief Payments Officer, Metrolinx Payments Canada Stakeholder Advisory Council Chair “We are very proud to contribute to this major milestone in the modernization of payments in Canada. This is a true collective effort, made possible through outstanding collaboration among the various industry stakeholders. This initiative demonstrates what we can achieve together to advance financial infrastructure for the benefit of businesses and Canadians.” Patrice Roy Head of Payments, National Bank Payments Canada Member Advisory Council Vice-Chair Key member program contributors “The Real-Time Rail is a powerful foundation for new business models, greater competition and economic growth across Canada. We're thrilled that Brim Financial is a future participant in Canada's Real-Time Rail. Brim's Payments-as-a-Service platform capabilities will enable real-time money movement, payments and intelligent commercial workflows in one unified ecosystem. This empowers our clients to accelerate innovation, unlock new opportunities, optimize liquidity and deliver transformative customer experiences.” Rasha Katabi, Founder and CEO Brim “The launch of the Real-Time Rail is a significant milestone in the modernization of Canada’s payment systems. Central 1 has invested in the infrastructure, capabilities and expertise to enable our clients to participate in real-time payments without the complexity to build and operate the underlying infrastructure themselves. Through that investment, we’re helping our clients unlock the benefits of real-time payments and extend those benefits to millions of Canadians.” Sunny Soin, Vice President, Product and Platform - Payments Central 1 “In today’s high-velocity commercial environment, there is need for instant, frictionless settlement backed by world-class technology. By deploying our proprietary Citi Payment Express platform for Canada’s Real-Time Rail, we are giving our clients immediate access to 24/7 real-time settlement and rich ISO 20022 remittance data via a high-availability, low-latency platform designed for instant payments. It is a powerful example of how Citi delivers global-standard technology to solve local market needs.” Mohneet Gujral, Head of Payments Citi Canada “Desjardins is proud to play a role modernizing Canada’s payment infrastructure. The Real-Time Rail will help us better serve the evolving payment needs of our members and clients, today and into the future.” Johanne Duhaime, Senior Executive Vice President, Technology and Organizational Performance Desjardins “The Real-Time Rail represents an important milestone for Canada and the continued modernization of our payment ecosystem. Real-time, always-on payments are changing how businesses move and manage money, from providing greater visibility and control over cash to enabling faster payouts and more seamless payment experiences for their customers. We’re proud to participate in this next chapter for Canadian payments and help our clients capture the opportunities it creates.” Dougal Middleton, Head of Payments and Treasury Services, Canada J.P. Morgan "The launch of the Real-Time Rail is an important milestone in the modernization of Canada's payment ecosystem. Meridian is proud to support this industry-wide effort and the development of payment infrastructure that will help enable faster, more modern payment experiences for Canadians and businesses across the country.” Matthew Seagrim, Chief Growth Officer Meridian Credit Union “The Real-Time Rail holds tremendous potential to empower Canadian consumers and businesses. I want to thank Payments Canada and Finance Canada for turning a sovereign real-time payments network into a reality. The imperative for made-in-Canada infrastructure that protects and supports Canadians, while strengthening domestic dependency, has never been more important. As adoption gains momentum, I look forward to seeing the positive impact that the RTR will have for workers, SMEs and homegrown innovation.” Dan Broten, Senior Vice President and Chief Digital Officer EQB Inc. (owner of President’s Choice Bank) Industry association collaboration “The CBA welcomes the implementation of the Real‑Time Rail, which will expand to include many of our members across Canada and will help modernize Canada’s payment systems and strengthen the backbone of the country’s financial market infrastructure. Innovation in payment technology continues to be a driving force behind payment choice and efficiency, thereby supporting economic growth in Canada. Security and trust remain paramount to the successful execution of real-time payments. Banks in Canada are dedicated to enabling a safe, fast and secure experience for individuals and businesses, while maintaining a resilient and stable financial system.” Anthony G. Ostler, President and CEO Canadian Bankers Association “The Real-Time Rail is a momentous transformation in how payments are done in Canada. Credit unions and their members will see real benefits, including improved convenience and better cash flow management for small businesses. As part of this phased implementation, we welcome the secure, flexible ways that credit unions will be able to participate in the RTR, so that very soon everyone who banks with a credit union or caisse populaire will experience faster, smarter and more flexible payments.” Jeff Guthrie, Chief Executive Officer Canadian Credit Union Association “Congratulations to Payments Canada on launching the Real-Time Rail. This is a milestone for small businesses, consumers and the innovators building Canada’s next generation of financial services. We look forward to seeing fintechs and financial institutions connect, bring more payments onto the rail and build services that give Canadians and businesses more choice.” Adriana Vega, Executive Director Fintechs Canada About Payments Canada Payments Canada enables prosperity, productivity and safety for Canada through trusted, critical national payment infrastructure. As a public-purpose organization, we own and operate: Lynx , our high-value payment system; the Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS), our retail batch payment system; and the Real-Time Rail (RTR), our new real-time payment system. We establish the by-laws, rules and standards that govern these systems, which cleared and settled $103 trillion in 2025 — more than $411 billion every business day. Transactions that pass through our systems include debit card payments, pre-authorized debits, direct deposits, bill payments, wire payments and cheques. In collaboration with our diverse membership, we continue to modernize Canada’s payment ecosystem to promote innovation, competition and deliver efficiencies that power a modern economy. title: Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game
body_text: Fable 5.2 One-Shotted My Nephew's Dream Game - NotesByLex.com Skip to content NotesByLex All posts Topics About Search notes / Fable 5.2 One-Shotted My Nephew's Dream Game LLMs can make complete multi-level games that are fun. Lex Toumbourou · Nov 10, 2026 GameProjects CodingAgents TL;DR - Fable 5.2 one-shotted my nephew's dream game from a bunch of drawings, and it's a lot of fun. You can try it here . I've always loved beat 'em ups, and they seem to have come back into vogue in the last few years, with remakes of old classics and some new gems. When my nephews visit, I use it as an excuse to try them out. Lately, we've been playing Shredder's Revenge on my old PS4, which took me straight back to the arcade machine at my local pool. One day, my younger nephew, Aiden, came to me with a proposal. Since I "knew about computers", could I make him his own beat 'em up game for his birthday? He had already drawn up the game design docs. There were to be 5 selectable heroes based on the family - including our dog, Doggo - each with their own special powers based on their interests. He had 12 bosses drawn up and a loose outline of a story. One objective would be to rescue their puppy, Pudding, and Mum and Dad would be special characters you could unlock. Heroes The Battle Wagon The villains, numbered 1st to 12th At the time - around January 2026 - building an indie game from scratch was a pretty unreasonable ask for a birthday present, and I did warn him to temper his expectations. Still, I thought it would be a fun exercise to test the agentic tools at my disposal. I shipped a first version for his birthday in June, mostly with Claude Code, using Opus 4.8 and Fable 5, and a side-scrolling template courtesy of AIOriented.dev . It worked, but it wasn't worth playing for more than a couple of minutes. The June version. Aiden was appreciative, but it clearly wasn't the game he'd imagined. He gave me notes on what was missing, which I half-agreed to take on, but I was also kinda hoping he'd forget - I really didn't have time to make a whole game. Unfortunately, he did not forget. Every time I saw him, he asked about the game. Enter: Fable 5.2 I was lucky enough to get an early look at Claude Fable 5.2 , and was told to try it on "my most ambitious use case". Finishing this game immediately sprang to mind. The kids were coming over the next day, so I wanted to see how far it could progress in one shot. Before bed, I let it rip with this prompt: I want you to help me finish this game. Make it as fun as possible. It should feel like a modern-day Ninja Turtles arcade game. An action-packed beat 'em up. Make the graphics amazing. You can use OpenAI's ChatGPT Images 2.5 for images. And ElevenLabs for sound effects. OpenAI key is /path/to/openai-key. ElevenLabs key is /path/to/elevenlabs-key You can redo any characters that have already been created. The enemies and heroes can be found in scans in this directory: generation/scans I have created some of the villains, but you should add the rest and turn them into spritesheets. Use any assets you find online. Create new sprites for the henchmen. Create backgrounds and power-ups in the levels. I'd like to plug in a controller so up to 4 people can play. Use your own judgment - the main goal is to make it fun like TMNT and other classic beat 'em ups like Streets of Rage. Make it one of the best games you can possibly make. You are a truly world-class game developer. Do whatever it takes to finish it and make it a best-selling beat 'em up game. Commit as you go. Don't worry about destroying what exists. Start fresh where it makes sense. Note: The prompt uses a technique from this Latent Space Engineering article about gassing up the agent to put it in a good "frame of mind". Not sure how relevant it is in the Fable 5.2 age, but hey - it didn't hurt. When I woke up, the game was waiting for me. And I couldn't believe my eyes! Fable had generated a game that was fun. Like, a lot of fun. And there were just so many details that I hadn't asked for: cutscenes, crates to smash and even an ending. It threw away most of my code and rewrote the game. It generated roughly 175 images and 140 audio clips. Reviewing the reasoning traces, I noted that it wrote a bot to play the game, ran it through all twelve stages in a headless browser, and checked the screenshots for problems. Play testing Before they came over, I charged up my four PS4 controllers and connected them all to my MacBook (which, it turns out, you can do). They worked perfectly. When they arrived, Aiden was absolutely delighted. "It's exactly as I imagined," he squealed. The afternoon shift Hulk Owen takes on Shellshock Everyone in A few rounds of playtesting, however, highlighted some deficiencies in the game. First, my older nephew, Owen, felt his character lacked a Hulk Smash move. Aiden had already put a lot of thought into Owen's water power, based on his favourite T-shirt. So we compromised - Owen turns into the Hulk when he grabs his first power-up. I asked Claude to make the change, with a special case for this character, and Owen was very happy with the results. Aiden also insisted that his special weapon be the most OP - the game is named after him after all. Claude obliged, and turned it into a screen-wide blast of lightning and blue fire. "Oh, that's perfect!" Aiden exclaimed. Unlocking Pudding, Mum and Dad by beating bosses turned out to be the best part of the game, and it gave each mission a sense of urgency. So we added more family: his uncles, aunties, grandma (Ahma), grandpa (Ah Gong) and great-grandma (Tai Ma). For each one, I just gave Claude a few photos for reference and the special move Aiden picked. When he couldn't decide, he had us call them up and ask what they wanted. Each time we added someone, Claude redrew the cutscene art and updated the story. Grandpa's Card Storm Grandma's Super Bloom Uncle Kev's Cheat Code On top of the human family, they decided that their pet turtles, Goldie and Billy, should be in the game as unlockable characters. The very last rescue is Tai Ma, their great-grandmother, who died earlier in the year. So Aiden suggested she should be an angel, and, again, Claude was happy to oblige. Five heroes became eighteen. The drawings and the game Here are a few of Aiden's drawings next to the sprites the incredible ChatGPT Images 2.5 made from them. Uncle Lex : "electric guitar". Doggo (my dog): she bites, and the spiky tail is her kick. The Battle Wagon : the villains steal it, which kicks off the whole game. Claude also decided that it should be an occasional power-up, where you grab the horn and it drives across the screen. That works. 8th: Shellshock . Aiden numbered his villains 1st to 12th, and the game uses that as the boss order. All 12 villains, drawing by sprite 1st: Dog Slayer 2nd: Rammox 3rd: Blazimp 4th: Bullzerk 5th: Beedrill 6th: Quadpunch 7th: Sensei Scowl 8th: Shellshock 9th: Corvax 10th: Shade 11th: Goldfist 12th: CrocoKing The final token tally The final token tally looked something like this: What was used Claude roughly 600 requests over two days: about 320M tokens read from cache, 19M written to cache, 1M output OpenAI images about 500 images: sprite sheets, character designs, portraits, backgrounds and key art ElevenLabs 11 music tracks, about 100 sound effects and 90 announcer lines So, call it 340M tokens for a 12-level, 18-character, four-player beat 'em up with original art, music and an announcer who shouts everyone's name. A pretty wild milestone I must admit I never tested this with Opus 5.5, so I'm not sure whether this was possible before Fable 5.2 rolled around. Still, whether it's thanks to this generation or the last, this is a pretty wild milestone. Claude Code with Fable 5.2 is capable of making entire 12-level fun games - in one shot. Try it yourself . Email Sign Up WHAT’S NEW NEWSLETTERS SECTIONS Daily Science Fixing Carbon Idea Watch Climate Parables PRINT EDITIONS Issue #1 Issue #2 Issue #3 Issue #4 Issue #5 Issue #6 Issue #7 Issue #8 ABOUT Team Anthropocene Archive Conservation Magazine Archive FAQs Awards Contact Us DAILY SCIENCE Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics’ cleverest trick yet See-through solar cells harvest some wavelengths of light to make electricity, while passing through the red and blue wavelengths that plants need. In a new agrivoltaics experiment, broccoli yields held steady. By Douglas Fox October 16, 2026 Let the best of Anthropocene come to you. Sign up for our free newsletters Success! Email Newsletters Newsletters Science Dispatch (weekly) Fixing Carbon (twice a month) Sign up Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them. A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels —without sacrificing the harvest. Agrivoltaic schemes— putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California . Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs. But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses. A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.   Recommended Reading: New study compares growing corn for energy to solar production. It’s no contest.   In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity. Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants. The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower. This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses. Lu et al. “ Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems .” Cell Reports Physical Science , 2026. Dismiss alert {{ message }} thisisme6598 gemini_files Repository navigation Code Issues Pull requests Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items gemini_files Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 1 ( 1 ) Star 18 ( 18 ) You must be signed in to star a repository About Documentation of Gemini File Leaking Behavior Resources Readme Activity Stars 18 stars Watchers 0 watching Forks 1 fork Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 3 Commits 3 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date README.md README.md View all files Repository files navigation README More items Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers" . Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost , Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see." Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic . Ingestion Pipeline When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups. Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic , running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios: Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query. Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight"). Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures. Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context. If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline --you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again. How to Reproduce Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings. Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better. Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about). If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above. To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history. I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number "]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers. Final Comments and Caveats Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data , including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject ). Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.
