x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link We’ve expanded our eighth generation TPU portfolio with TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, marking four new TPU systems in a single year. Amin Vahdat SVP and Chief Technologist, AI and Infrastructure Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We’re expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows. These systems help you manage complex agentic workloads by providing specialized hardware for security, density, and reasoning. You can learn more about these additions and our latest software updates by watching our broadcast or visiting the Google Cloud website to explore our full infrastructure lineup. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with the new TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max systems. TPU 8tx provides hardware-level security for sensitive data, while TPU 8i Max handles massive context windows. These systems join TPU 8t and TPU 8i to offer specialized performance for every AI lifecycle stage. We are making TPUs more accessible by supporting PyTorch, open-source software, and automated tools for developers. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further, expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference. This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack. Opening up TPUs to every developer When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code. Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware. This investment comes together today across these key areas: Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU , so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs. Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks , which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further. Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our agents more resource-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends and resumes idle sessions, cutting operational infrastructure costs. Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer (TPU Sync): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync , the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%. Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils , you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding. Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs. Co-designing with a decade of experience Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side. Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT. title: What is malloc doing, anyway?
body_text: What is malloc doing, anyway? | Ben M. Andrew Skip to content Ben M. Andrew Blog Publications Projects Teaching Art Menu ; Safari, which supports neither, warms the HTTP cache with a low-priority fetch. A single shared listener collects the selectors from every include on the page; Chromium bails out early so it never double-fetches. The call below passes the selector through `json`, not wrapped in quotes of our own. Interpolated bare into a single-quoted literal, the header's `a[href^='/']` closed the string on its own apostrophe and the whole script was a SyntaxError — inert, and invisible, because the only browsers that reach this line are the ones with no native support to fall back from. --> What is malloc doing, anyway? Published Nov 8, 2026 malloc has a very nice and simple interface: you ask for a certain amount of memory, and you’re given a void pointer to your block of contiguous bytes that’s been magicked into existence. Once you’re done with it, you call free with the same pointer and the memory disappears into the ether. But what’s actually happening here? Obviously, as we’re running as a userspace program, malloc must be asking the kernel for the memory through syscalls . However, we may be allocating many small blocks, and syscalls are expensive (575 ns for an empty one, as measured below), so some bookkeeping is done in the background. We’ll demonstrate this on GNU libc ( glibc ) with the program snippet below, which calls malloc(16) a thousand times. static void * ptrs [ 1000 ] ; int main ( void ) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < 1000 ; i ++ ) ptrs [ i ] = malloc ( 16 ) ; } Using strace , we can see that the whole loop makes only two brk syscalls: the first asks where the program break is (the address where the process’s heap ends), and the second grows the heap by 132 KiB. These are both done in the first malloc call — the other 999 just take from that already allocated memory. $ strace -e trace = brk,mmap,munmap,write \ ./malloc1000 > /dev/null ... brk(NULL) = 0x59faca231000 brk(0x59faca252000) = 0x59faca252000 +++ exited with 0 +++ You may see both brk and sbrk mentioned in discussions. brk is a syscall that sets the program break to the address it is provided, and sbrk is a libc convenience wrapper that takes a delta , increasing the program break by that amount. The Address Space # A running process gets its own address space , split into a number of regions. These include text for executable code, data for initialised global variables, and bss for uninitialised global variables, among others. The following program prints one address from each region of the process. # define SHOW ( label , p ) \ printf ( "%-22s %p\n" , label , ( void * ) ( p ) ) SHOW ( "main (text)" , main ) ; SHOW ( "initialised (data)" , & initialised ) ; SHOW ( "uninitialised (bss)" , & uninitialised ) ; SHOW ( "malloc(16) (heap)" , malloc ( 16 ) ) ; SHOW ( "program break" , sbrk ( 0 ) ) ; SHOW ( "printf (libc)" , printf ) ; SHOW ( "local (stack)" , & local ) ; The addresses rise from the binary’s code up to its stack. $ ./layout main (text) 0x59c0791d7149 initialised (data) 0x59c0791da020 uninitialised (bss) 0x59c0791da028 malloc(16) (heap) 0x59c0903182b0 program break 0x59c090338000 printf (libc) 0x711dcf7c15b0 local (stack) 0x7ffff86c45ec Some of these regions can change as the program runs. For example, malloc(16) grows the heap and moves the break up. Note that in this run, the break and printf in libc are 23.4 TiB apart, about 1,530 times the machine’s 15.6 GiB of RAM. Nearly all of that range is unmapped, so it costs no physical memory. low high at start text data BSS gap break 23 TiB unmapped libc stack malloc(16) text data BSS gap heap break 23 TiB unmapped libc stack A Toy Allocator with sbrk # Because we can move the program break directly, we can write a little allocator of our own. This is called a bump allocator, because each call simply bumps up the amount of memory that we are allowed to use. void * my_malloc ( size_t size ) { void * p = sbrk ( align_up ( size ) ) ; return p == ( void * ) - 1 ? NULL : p ; } void my_free ( void * ptr ) { ( void ) ptr ; } This allocator is not very good! It moves the break on every single request, and each move is a syscall. We can time a syscall against malloc to see why malloc requests large blocks from the kernel and cuts them up itself. Each of the following three functions is timed over a million calls. static void * volatile sink ; static void call_getppid ( void ) { syscall ( SYS_getppid ) ; } static void call_sbrk ( void ) { sink = sbrk ( 16 ) ; } static void call_malloc ( void ) { sink = malloc ( 16 ) ; } sbrk(16) costs only 35 ns more than the empty syscall, whereas malloc(16) runs 22.7 times faster than sbrk(16) . $ ./syscall-cost syscall(SYS_getppid) 575.2 ns per call sbrk(16) 610.1 ns per call malloc(16) 26.9 ns per call sbrk(16) / malloc(16) 22.7x The bump allocator also has no way to reuse freed memory. Each request lands straight after the one before, so in the following example, d goes after c even though b has been freed. $ ./my-bump-1 a = my_malloc(16) start+0 b = my_malloc(1) start+16 c = my_malloc(100) start+32 my_free(b) d = my_malloc(1) start+144 break start+160 The rest of the post improves the allocator one stage at a time. Chunks and Headers # malloc actually allocates more memory than you request. This is because each allocation, or chunk , has a size header just before the returned pointer; this is how free works without passing an explicit size. Chunk sizes are always multiples of 16, so the low bits of the size are always zero, and glibc keeps three flags in them. header 24 bytes for the caller header p = malloc(24) next chunk chunk : 32 bytes size = 32 0 A 0 M 1 P one 8-byte word A : another arena M : own mapping P : chunk before in use size_t requests [ ] = { 1 , 24 , 25 , 1000 } ; size_t count = sizeof requests / sizeof requests [ 0 ] ; for ( size_t i = 0 ; i < count ; i ++ ) { char * p = malloc ( requests [ i ] ) ; size_t chunk = ( ( size_t * ) p ) [ - 1 ] & ~ ( size_t ) 7 ; printf ( "%8zu %8zu\n" , requests [ i ] , chunk ) ; } Each chunk is the request plus 8 bytes for the header, rounded up to a multiple of 16, with a minimum of 32. The rounding keeps every pointer that malloc returns 16-byte aligned, which is the alignment x86-64 gives max_align_t , so the memory suits any C type. The 32-byte minimum leaves room for the list pointers that a chunk stores once it is freed. $ ./chunk-header request chunk 1 32 24 32 25 48 1000 1008 When we free a chunk, it is put into what’s called a free list to allow reuse. When more data is requested, malloc looks through this free list and splits large chunks to fit small requests, and free merges free neighbours back together. Each chunk in the free list needs two pieces of information: its size (which we already have), and a pointer to the next chunk in the free list. glibc stores the pointer after the size, reusing the memory that the user stored their data in before it was freed! The toy allocator stores the same two fields in each chunk. typedef struct chunk { size_t size ; struct chunk * next ; } chunk_t ; Splitting and Coalescing # We can improve our my_malloc by rounding the request plus its header up to a multiple of 16 bytes, and taking the first chunk in the free list that is big enough. To keep things simple, the toy’s header is the whole chunk_t , so a chunk keeps room for next even while it is in use. That makes the header 16 bytes where glibc ’s is 8, and my_malloc(100) takes a 128-byte chunk where malloc(100) takes 112. void * my_malloc ( size_t size ) { size_t need = align_up ( size + HEADER_SIZE , ALIGN ) ; for ( chunk_t * * link = & free_list ; * link != NULL ; link = & ( * link ) -> next ) if ( ( * link ) -> size >= need ) return take ( link , need ) ; if ( grow_heap ( need ) != 0 ) return NULL ; return my_malloc ( size ) ; } We define take to split that chunk, leaving whatever the request does not need in the free list. static void * take ( chunk_t * * link , size_t need ) { chunk_t * c = * link ; if ( c -> size > need ) { chunk_t * rest = ( chunk_t * ) ( ( char * ) c + need ) ; rest -> size = c -> size - need ; rest -> next = c -> next ; c -> size = need ; * link = rest ; } else { * link = c -> next ; } return ( char * ) c + HEADER_SIZE ; } When no free chunk fits, grow_heap moves the program break up in 64 KiB steps using sbrk and puts the new space on the free list as one chunk. With headers, we can now actually implement a proper my_free function! It steps back from the pointer to the header and hands the chunk c to insert_free . That function walks the list to find the free chunks either side of c by address, prev and next , and links c in between them. Then, if c ends where next starts, or starts where prev ends, the two become one chunk. if ( next != NULL && ( char * ) c + c -> size == ( char * ) next ) { c -> size += next -> size ; c -> next = next -> next ; } if ( prev != NULL && ( char * ) prev + prev -> size == ( char * ) c ) { prev -> size += c -> size ; prev -> next = c -> next ; } A test program allocates a , b and c , frees a and b , allocates d , then frees the rest. a , b and c allocated a b c 65056 free_list my_free(a) 128 b c 65056 free_list my_free(b) merges a and b 352 c 65056 free_list d = my_malloc(50) splits the merged chunk d 272 c 65056 free_list my_free(c) merges both neighbours d 65456 free_list my_free(d) 65536 free_list Each line shows the chunk that the call allocated, if any, and then the free list. Every chunk is an [offset, size] pair counted from the start of the heap, and the offset is where its header starts, 16 bytes before the pointer that my_malloc returns. $ ./my-freelist-2 a = my_malloc(100) [0, 128] free: [128, 65408] b = my_malloc(200) [128, 224] free: [352, 65184] c = my_malloc(100) [352, 128] free: [480, 65056] my_free(a) free: [0, 128] [480, 65056] my_free(b) free: [0, 352] [480, 65056] d = my_malloc(50) [0, 80] free: [80, 272] [480, 65056] my_free(c) free: [80, 65456] my_free(d) free: [0, 65536] d gets the chunk at offset 0, split from the 352-byte chunk that a and b merged into. The bump allocator put its fourth request after everything else. Freeing c merges three chunks into one, and freeing d leaves the single 64 KiB chunk that grow_heap added. Demand Paging # my_free reuses memory, but it never returns any to the kernel. Whether a free chunk still costs RAM depends on when the kernel puts physical memory behind an address. Each process sees virtual memory , which the kernel maps onto physical RAM in 4 KiB pages . That separation allows the kernel to hand out address ranges with no physical RAM behind them — a virtual page only needs to be backed by physical memory on its first write . after sbrk : 8 pages added, none resident virtual physical after writing 3 pages : 3 faults, 3 resident virtual physical The following program moves the break up by 1 GiB, then writes one byte to every page and prints a row after each 256 MiB. char * p = sbrk ( SIZE ) ; print_row ( 0 ) ; for ( size_t offset = 0 ; offset < SIZE ; offset += PAGE_SIZE ) { p [ offset ] = 1 ; if ( ( offset + PAGE_SIZE ) % ( SIZE / 4 ) == 0 ) print_row ( ( long ) ( ( offset + PAGE_SIZE ) >> 20 ) ) ; } Virtual size counts the addresses the process has mapped, and resident set size (RSS) counts the pages that are in RAM. Straight after sbrk , virtual size is already just over 1 GiB, while RSS is 1308 KiB. Each 256 MiB written then costs 65,536 page faults, one per 4 KiB page, increasing the RSS. $ ./demand-paging written faults virtual resident 0 MiB 3 1050916 KiB 1308 KiB 256 MiB 65539 1050916 KiB 263536 KiB 512 MiB 131075 1050916 KiB 525680 KiB 768 MiB 196611 1050916 KiB 787824 KiB 1024 MiB 262147 1050916 KiB 1049968 KiB Once a chunk’s pages have been written, they stay resident after my_free , until the allocator gives them back to the kernel. Giving Memory Back # We give memory back to the kernel by lowering the break. We introduce a new function, trim , that lowers the break once the free chunk at the top of the heap reaches 128 KiB, keeping 64 KiB so that the next few requests don’t move the break straight back up. static void trim ( void ) { chunk_t * top = free_list ; if ( top == NULL ) return ; while ( top -> next != NULL ) top = top -> next ; char * end = ( char * ) top + top -> size ; if ( end != ( char * ) sbrk ( 0 ) || top -> size < TRIM_THRESHOLD ) return ; size_t release = ( top -> size - TOP_PAD ) / PAGE_SIZE * PAGE_SIZE ; top -> size -= release ; sbrk ( - ( intptr_t ) release ) ; } A test program allocates 1 MiB and then a 16-byte chunk above it, then writes to every page of the 1 MiB block. ( Anonymous RSS counts resident memory with no backing file, which keeps libc ’s code out of the numbers.) $ ./my-trim-3 break anonymous RSS my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16) start+1088 KiB 1124 KiB my_free(1 MiB) start+1088 KiB 1124 KiB my_free(16) start+64 KiB 160 KiB Freeing the 1 MiB block leaves the break at 1088 KiB and anonymous RSS at 1124 KiB, because the 16-byte chunk above it is still live. Once that chunk goes too, trim lowers the break to 64 KiB, dropping the anonymous RSS to 160 KiB. Only the top of the heap can be given back. A live chunk holds the break above it, so every free chunk below it stays resident, as the 1 MiB block did here. Over a long run, many allocations and deallocations leave free gaps between live chunks that later requests rarely fill, which is called fragmentation . These gaps stay resident, so in a long-running program, fragmentation can grow RSS until a memory limit kills the process. live chunk free chunk, or wholly free page page holding part of a live chunk all chunks freed … break all but the last freed … break every other chunk freed … break Large Blocks with mmap # The mmap syscall usually maps a file into the address space. With the MAP_ANONYMOUS flag there is no backing file, and the kernel creates a zero-filled, page-aligned mapping anywhere in the address space. Like the heap, its resident pages count towards the anonymous RSS. The munmap syscall returns a block with its own mapping to the kernel as soon as it is freed, whatever lies next to it. To integrate this into our own allocator, my_malloc chooses between sbrk and mmap by the size of the request. Any request of 128 KiB or more, header included, gets a mapping of its own from map_chunk , rounded up to whole pages; smaller requests take the existing sbrk free list path. static void * map_chunk ( size_t need ) { size_t len = align_up ( need , PAGE_SIZE ) ; chunk_t * c = mmap ( NULL , len , PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE , MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS , - 1 , 0 ) ; if ( c == MAP_FAILED ) return NULL ; c -> size = len | MMAPPED ; // chunk is mapped return ( char * ) c + HEADER_SIZE ; } For mmap ped chunks, we use one of the three flags in the size header (M) to record that this chunk has its own mapping. my_free checks this bit to know how to free it. It unmaps a mapped chunk with munmap , and puts any other chunk back on the free list, where trim can release it. void my_free ( void * ptr ) { if ( ptr == NULL ) return ; chunk_t * c = ( chunk_t * ) ( ( char * ) ptr - HEADER_SIZE ) ; if ( c -> size & MMAPPED ) { munmap ( c , c -> size & ~ ( size_t ) MMAPPED ) ; return ; } insert_free ( c ) ; trim ( ) ; } Running the previous demo again, we see that freeing the 1 MiB block drops the anonymous RSS while the 16-byte chunk is still live. $ ./my-mmap-4 break anonymous RSS my_malloc(1 MiB), my_malloc(16) start+64 KiB 1128 KiB my_free(1 MiB) start+64 KiB 100 KiB my_free(16) start+64 KiB 100 KiB The following diagram shows how this might look in the address space. low high before text data BSS gap heap break unmapped libc stack my_malloc(1 MiB) text data BSS gap heap break unmapped 1 MiB libc stack my_free(1 MiB) text data BSS gap heap break unmapped libc stack Why not mmap everything? Some allocators do! Even glibc creates extra heaps, called arenas , with mmap , and spreads threads across them so that they don’t all contend for the lock on the main heap. However, separate mappings have separate regions with no guarantee of contiguity, and chunks can’t be coalesced across these gaps. On the other hand, allocating with sbrk just bumps up the one contiguous region that you already have. A freed chunk that stays on the heap keeps its pages resident, so reusing it causes no page faults. Each new mapping starts with no physical memory behind it, and faults on every page it writes. Comparing Performance # We compare the performance of our allocators against glibc ’s malloc with a workload that repeatedly allocates and deallocates blocks of varying sizes 1 . To measure the speed, we find the average time of a step : free a random live block, allocate a replacement of random size, and write to each of its pages. At the end of the run, the live blocks hold 10.3 MiB. The last two columns give the anonymous RSS at that point, and again after every block is freed, which is the memory the allocator keeps. Allocator Average time per step (µs) Anonymous RSS, blocks live (MiB) Anonymous RSS, all freed (MiB) my-bump-1 1.72 1425 1425 my-freelist-2 5.12 17.8 17.8 my-trim-3 11.2 14.5 0.188 my-mmap-4 11.8 11.2 0.188 glibc 0.0789 19.0 19.0 my-bump-1 never frees or reuses memory, so its RSS is the 1425 MiB that the run allocates in total. Its 1.72 µs per step comes from an sbrk call for every request and page faults on new pages. my-freelist-2 reuses memory, so its RSS of 17.8 MiB is much closer to the 10.3 MiB of live data. However, each step walks the list twice: my_malloc walks it to find a fit, and insert_free walks it to find the chunk’s neighbours. my-trim-3 adds a third walk, because trim looks for the last free chunk on every my_free . my-freelist-2 and my-trim-3 run 65 and 142 times slower than glibc respectively. In return, my-trim-3 keeps only 0.188 MiB once every block is freed. my-mmap-4 calls mmap for large requests, which raises its time per step to 11.8 µs but gives it the lowest RSS with blocks live, at 11.2 MiB. Why is glibc so fast? The slowdowns in our allocators are due to having to walk a long free list of chunks multiple times. glibc instead keeps free chunks in bins , separate lists by size, so a request can walk a list of appropriately sized chunks directly. It also keeps up to seven freed chunks of each small size in a thread-local cache (tcache) and hands them straight back to the next request of that size. The tcache also explains the last column, where glibc keeps 19.0 MiB after every block is freed. The heap counts a cached chunk as in use, so one near the top stops glibc from lowering the break. The GLIBC_TUNABLES environment variable can turn the tcache off with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0 , or fix the mmap threshold at 128 KiB with GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=131072 . Allocator Average time per step (µs) Anonymous RSS, blocks live (MiB) Anonymous RSS, all freed (MiB) glibc 0.0789 19.0 19.0 glibc , tcache_count=0 0.121 17.4 0.250 glibc , mmap_threshold=131072 0.843 12.1 5.85 With the tcache off, freeing everything leaves 0.250 MiB, and each step takes 1.5 times as long as before. glibc makes 51 mmap calls in the whole run, against the 5040 that my-mmap-4 makes. Freeing a mapped chunk raises glibc ’s threshold to that chunk’s size, so later large requests come from the heap. With the threshold fixed at 128 KiB, every large request pays for its syscalls and page faults again, and glibc runs 10.7 times slower. malloc spends memory to stay away from the kernel, parcelling out large blocks in userspace so that most calls never make a syscall. Links # Reproducible snippets for each program ( link ). glibc ’s own description of its allocator’s internals, covering chunks, bins, arenas and the tcache ( link ). The man pages for brk(2) and sbrk(2) ( link ), mmap(2) ( link ), mallopt(3) ( link ) and malloc_trim(3) ( link ). The benchmark keeps 4000 blocks live, and each step frees a random block and allocates a replacement of a random size. Of the requests, 90% are 16 to 512 bytes, 9% are up to 16 KiB, and 1% are 128 KiB to 256 KiB. Each new block gets one write per page. An allocator runs 500,000 steps in a fresh process, built at -O2 . Run on an Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3. ↩︎ Liked this? title: Muse Ember: Our smallest, most efficient model
body_text: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Skip to main content AI Research AI Developers Try Muse Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember November 9, 2026 · 4 minute read Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps. Foundation for wrongful termination, discrimination Share this: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit Share on X (Opens in new window) X By Shelly Bradbury | sbradbury@denverpost.com | The Denver Post PUBLISHED: November 6, 2026 at 4:00 AM MST Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years. The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation , a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum , a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds. And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge. Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide. When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge. Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings. Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.” Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.” An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit. Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide. “I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.” Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version. This screenshot from a federal lawsuit shows a so-called 'suicide pledge' distributed to employees at The Ethereum Foundation as part of a document outlining the organization's vision for the future. (Screenshot via U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado) The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit. When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit. After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.” Suicide prevention resources Colorado Crisis Line : 1-844-493-8255, coloradocrisisservices.org . Chat online or text TALK to 38255. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline Dial 988 for national hotline. Mental Health First Aid : mhfaco.org . Get trained to recognize the signs and how to respond. American Foundation for Suicide Prevention : afsp.org . Join one of their upcoming walks for awareness in Colorado. Crisis Text Line : crisistextline.org . Text 741741 from anywhere in the nation to reach a counselor. It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.” In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit. Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit. “If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair. The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated. Related Articles Crypto wants its shine back The crypto world can’t wait for “the Merge” Crypto convention sues Denver company over “subpar” show Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies. One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself. Get more Colorado news by signing up for our daily Your Morning Dozen email newsletter. title: When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385
body_text: When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385 - CNX Software Skip to content CNX Software – Embedded Systems News Reviews, tutorials and the latest news about embedded systems, IoT, open-source hardware, SBC's, microcontrollers, processors, and more Menu About About Us Contact Us Advertisement & Consulting Services Work for Us Support CNX Software Privacy Policy All News Raspberry Pi Arduino Reviews Tutorials UP Embedded UP AI Ecosystem Embedded Boards Embedded Systems DEBIX Posted on November 3, 2026 by Jean-Luc Aufranc (CNXSoft) - 22 Comments on When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385 When will this stop? The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB SBC now sells for $385 Raspberry Pi has announced yet another price increase , this time for most models with 16GB of RAM. The Raspberry Pi 5 16GB now sells for $385, an $80 increase compared to the last price hike in April , and the Raspberry Pi CM5 system-on-module gets a $40 increase, starting at $375 for the Lite model without wireless. The “good news” is that the Raspberry Pi 500+ mechanical keyboard PC stays at the same price, starting at $410. I suppose they can afford it on that model, because it’s already richly priced and the demand must be lower than for single board computers and compute modules. Here’s the updated price list for the Compute Module 5 16GB variants. Part number eMMC Wireless Price CM5016000 0GB (Lite) No $375 CM5016016 16GB No $400 CM5016032 32GB No $410 CM5016064 64GB No $410 CM5116000 0GB (Lite) Yes $380 CM5116016 16GB Yes $405 CM5116032 32GB Yes $415 CM5116064 64GB Yes $415 Interestingly, the price is the same whether we get 32GB or 64GB eMMC flash. I still remember people complaining about the $120 launch price of the Raspberry Pi 5 16GB . That was less than two years ago, and that price would feel like a bargain today. Of course, Raspberry Pi isn’t the only company impacted by high RAM prices this year. Here’s a recent list of price hikes for popular SBCs and SoMs: April 1, 2026 – A ll Raspberry Pi boards with 4GB RAM or more get a price increase . The Raspberry Pi 4 3GB is launched to compensate somewhat. July 22, 2026 – NVIDIA increases the price of Jetson modules and devkits by up to 101% October 1, 2026 – Raspberry Pi 4/5 2GB boards aren’t immune and also get a price hike . October 19, 2026 – The Arduino VENTUNO Q now sells for $399 instead of $299. In all fairness, the latter was an introductory price, so the higher retail price was expected. Of course, all other vendors like Orange Pi, Radxa, Hardkernel, Banana Pi, and so on, also had their own price increases, just not as broadly advertised across the web. So when will this all end? It’s hard to know. Micron expects the RAM shortage to last at least until 2028 , and SK Hynix thinks it could only be resolved sometime in 2030 . On the flip side, the stock prices of memory vendors have cratered in recent months, as investors worry about the sustainability of profits, which could signal cracks in the current cycle. Some of their customers also struggle to get financing as the price of tokens keeps collapsing, and the profitability of AI is put into question.  The war in the Middle East is also a wildcard, as critical materials (e.g., helium) required for the manufacturing of wafers and chips could also experience shortages. We’ll have to wait and see. Thanks to TLS and Anonymous for the tip. Today’s high prices will eventually fall, DRAM will get denser, daily use requirements not involving local AI probably won’t scale up with the density/capacity increases. title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
body_text: unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world shubs Co-founder of Assetnote, security researcher. Assetnote Home Github Twitter LinkedIn unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world November 7 2026 I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform. Having looked at platforms like this before ( previous works ), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker". When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet. The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made. Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au : dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ... Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au . What else existed under this domain? The admin tool Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story. One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it? Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in. I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do. Oozing quality Who even reads JavaScript bundles? Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle. For example, we could look up user accounts by email address: But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that. In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites. This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain. Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that: With the subscriber GUID, you could pull the full account details (including the user's email via the /v1/account endpoint) like so: Well, I guess we have the first part of our chain sorted. Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> User Account PII (email) registered on the automaker's identity platform (ForgeRock OpenIDM). Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle. The identity platform Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate. When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au , and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc). So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for. The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au , we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au . This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform. This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱: Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too. Fighting the WAF Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/* . Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible). Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway. I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be? Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/ , and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work: At least we know the credentials work in production But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/ , thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so: Gosh, we're so close?! In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT. We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully. All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following: Maybe there is a whitelist for some endpoints? These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way? /openidm/endpoint/aaa -> 403 WAF blocked /openidm/endpoint/pinService -> 404, no WAF block Interesting! What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail , guid , and phone . Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do? Eep. The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded. Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre. Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it. It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination. When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/ , we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue. Taking over accounts With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile: PATCH /static%2f..%2fopenidm/managed/user/f7ba554REDACTED HTTP/1.1 Host: openidm.redacted-identity.com.au X-OpenIDM-Username: idmadmin X-OpenIDM-Password: REDACTED X-OpenIDM-NoSession: true Content-Type: application/json If-Match: "0000000abc123..." Cache-Control: no-store Accept: application/json [{"operation":"replace","field":"/password","value":"Testing123!"}] Which responded with: > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > {"_id":"f7ba554REDACTED","_rev":"0000000def456..."} OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication? Skipping MFA Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app: POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded grant_type=password& [email protected] &password=Testing123!&client_id=REDACTED_PORTAL&client_secret=REDACTED > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "access_token": "...", > "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...", > "token_type": "Bearer", > "expires_in": 3599 > } We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session: POST /json/realms/REDACTED/authenticate?authIndexType=service&authIndexValue=IDTokenROPC HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json Accept-API-Version: resource=2.0, protocol=1.0 idtoken: eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi... > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "tokenId": "AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*", > "successUrl": "/openam/console", > "realm": "/REDACTED" > } Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token: POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/authorize HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0 x-fr-version: 2025.05.05 Authorization: Basic <REDACTED> iPlanetDirectoryPro: AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* Cookie: iPlanetDirectoryPro=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* client_id=REDACTED_APP&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&scope=openid%20profile%20write&response_type=code&state=<state>&code_challenge=<S256_challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&decision=allow&csrf=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...* > HTTP/1.1 302 Found > Location: com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state> POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1 Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0 Authorization: Basic <REDACTED> grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&client_id=REDACTED_APP&code_verifier=<pkce_verifier> > HTTP/1.1 200 OK > { > "access_token": "<app_access_token>", > "refresh_token": "...", > "token_type": "Bearer", > "scope": "openid profile write", > "expires_in": 3599 > } It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app. Unlocking the car At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone. POST /v1/remote/route/command HTTP/1.1 Host: api.redacted-telematics.com.au Authorization: Bearer <app_access_token> X-API-KEY: REDACTED X-GUID: f7ba554REDACTED X-BRAND: REDACTED X-APPBRAND: REDACTED X-CHANNEL: REDACTED X-LOCALE: en-AU X-APPVERSION: REDACTED X-OSNAME: Android X-OSVERSION: 14 X-DEVICE-TIMEZONE: AEST X-CORRELATIONID: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8 X-GENERATION: REDACTED VIN: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json User-Agent: okhttp/4.12.0 {"command": "door-unlock", "autoFixPopup": false, "beepCount": null} And magic. The doors unlocked. We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with. But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this: Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> OpenIDM admin credentials in JS vendor bundle -> Path traversal to bypass the WAF -> MFA bypass via ROPC flow -> Minting a consumer app token -> Remote command API. At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these. 0:00 / 0:57 1× You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives? There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here . It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments. At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

title: KetchUp – Open-source SketchUp alternative built with Rust and WebGPU
body_text: BenchUp — Free 3D Woodworking & Furniture Design App Skip to content BenchUp . GitHub ↗ Try in browser ↗ 3D design for your next woodworking project. BenchUp is a free, open-source 3D modeling app for woodworking and furniture design. Plan a shelf, table, cabinet, or workbench with exact measurements before you build. Use it on Windows, macOS, Linux, or right in your desktop browser. A little sketch. A whole new dimension. Actual BenchUp workspace Download for Windows ↓ Windows x64 · .exe installer Download for macOS ↓ Apple Silicon · .pkg installer Download for Linux ↓ Linux x64 · AppImage Release notes & all downloads ↗ Free & open source. No account needed. Made for a desktop browser and a mouse. From the first line to the finer details. Start with a simple shape. Keep the tools you need close, and your model at the center. ↗ Draw. Pull. Make it yours. Sketch lines, rectangles, circles, and freehand outlines. Turn faces into forms with Push/Pull, then move, scale, offset, and paint. ⌖ Keep your ideas in measure. Snap to geometry and axes, type exact lengths, and add dimensions. Organize the bigger picture with groups, components, and tags. ↓ Your work, in your hands. Autosave locally and download portable .ketchup projects. Import SketchUp geometry or export an OBJ to take your model further. Plan your furniture before the first cut. For woodworkers, furniture makers, and DIY builders who want to explore a project in 3D. Model the pieces Draw board outlines with rectangles and lines, then use Push/Pull to give them thickness. Move and copy geometry to explore shelves, tables, cabinets, workbenches, and other furniture. Check dimensions and fit Enter exact lengths, snap to geometry and axes, and use Tape Measure and Dimensions to inspect your design. Orbit around the assembly to review proportions before taking it to the workshop. Keep the project organized Use groups, reusable components, and tags to organize parts. Save a portable .ketchup project locally, import SketchUp geometry, or export OBJ geometry for another 3D workflow. Start with the browser editor or download the desktop app . Read the user guide for modeling instructions and supported workflows. Your first shape is three steps away. The editor opens with a clean slate. Here’s a good place to start. Open the workspace ↗ Draw a rectangle Click one corner, then the opposite corner to create your first face. Give it some depth Choose Push/Pull, click the face, move your mouse, and click to finish. Find a fresh perspective Choose Orbit and drag to look around. Scroll to zoom; press F to fit your model. A few things before you begin. What do I need to run it? A desktop browser with hardware acceleration and WebGPU or WebGL2 support. Use a mouse and keyboard for modeling. You can also run BenchUp as a native Windows, macOS, or Linux app. Where does my work go? Your model is autosaved in this browser on this device. Use File → Save to download a .ketchup project you can keep or open again. Clearing browser data can remove autosaved work, so download projects you want to keep. There’s no cloud storage or account to set up. Can I use my existing models? Use File → Import/Export to import SketchUp (.skp) geometry or export Wavefront OBJ (.obj). Imports run locally. SketchUp textures, scenes, and some model features aren’t supported; OBJ export includes geometry without materials. Is BenchUp free? Yes. BenchUp is open source under the MIT license and written in Rust. Explore the code, read the full guide, or contribute on GitHub. A blank canvas. Plenty of possibilities. Let’s make something ↗ Prefer the desktop? Download BenchUp ↑ BenchUp . Free 3D modeling for woodworking and furniture design. Source & documentation MIT license Application facts Sitemap

title: Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026)
body_text: Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026) | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Ask HN: What are you working on? (November 2026) 280 points by david927 1 day ago | hide | past | favorite | 978 comments What are you working on? What have you been curious about lately?   help jzig 1 day ago | next [–] I was laid off a few weeks ago. Then I learned my dad’s carpet cleaning company has been struggling, so I started learning about Google Local Service Ads to help him out. THEN I learned his old Windows desktop CRM was discontinued and one OS update away from no longer working. I wanted a way to track every dollar spent to determine return on ad spend, but the Google LSA dashboard left a lot to be desired. And existing SaaS CRMs didn’t have great integrations to Google Ads API. So I built Crewbird, a Field Service Management and CRM for service based businesses with Google LSA integration where my dad is quickly approaching 3x ROAS! I’m still looking for work in the mean time but I’m proud of what I’ve achieved so far. https://getcrewbird.com/ reply tropicalhunter 1 day ago | parent | next [–] Man, I would love to know more about this. The space between a full blown ERP and a tracker on an Excel Spreadsheet is absolutely abysmal. Then when you start introducing things like fleet and field crew management on top of the procurement, account management and AR/AP while acting as a full blown salesman that a lot of middle managers are being expected to do right now, it gets absolutely soul crushing to swap between 12 different trackers per hour just to find a snippet of the information you are looking for. I have something vibed together as an internal tool that does well enough, but definitely not something I would ever refer to as a CRM by any stretch of the imagination and the bridge between basic on-the-shelf inventory and tracking rental assets are two completely different beasts. Maybe more of a prettier version of the spreadsheets we already use with more automated functionality would be more apt. reply jzig 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] Thanks for one of the only positive comments here. There are still areas for improvement but it has proven useful so far. Happy to talk any time. reply skrig 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Building this right now! I've helped several companies implement CRMs and worked on heavily customizing my ERP at work. They all suck, bad. 90% of companies only need something simple. I'll let you know when I'm finished, would be awesome to get some feedback if you're willing. reply tropicalhunter 1 day ago | root | parent | next [–] All horrible. Some of those modular CRM's seemed promising, but still felt like we would end up with oversaturated feature sets and would just be trading one suite for another and the same problems. Definitely share when you do. If you have a repo or anything that I can follow while it is still in development, that would be great. reply Teever 9 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] Have you tried using Odoo and if so what didn’t you like about it? reply calvinmorrison 1 day ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] or better to say different people need different things. a accountant is more interested in properly calculating the COGs than the guy inputting his labor and goods on a ticket. reply xeonax 14 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] My slop attempt at this https://worx.aeonax.com/ . I felt there was a gap, an absence of high bureaucracy software. So made above. People I know did check it out. so theres that. reply minierpthrowawa 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] I actually did this for my father’s industry in 2016. Took a break from my sales job, and built him a project management tool about 25% of the way to an ERP tool. I’ve sold a few monthly recurring accounts to other companies and overall the people that like it enough to finish onboarding seem to like it. Watch out though.. don’t work too hard too long for too little just for dad. Him being your #1 user that loves you can make you keep going longer than you would if you had to face reality. My real advice… start working for him and using the software yourself 100%. Even for $5 an hour so you both have skin in the game. Him to have some help, you to learn, but the money adds a bit of reality so neither of you do things only because it’s free or because it’s family. My saas has improved leaps and bounds this year when I started to work in the industry for a company actually using my product. I learned things I never saw by just giving demos. reply vablings 12 hours ago | root | parent | next [–] There are so many corporate bone piles due to the disconnect with how a software ought to work and how designers take that specification and make it. I think at every place I have worked under several different projects the development team have always never really aligned correctly with the people using the software every day (internal tooling not for sale saas or product). Its really not hard to sit down and listen to users but I have encountered such massive egos and resistances to simple moving a button somewhere else or changing a flow or behavior to be easier to use for a layman that the juice is never worth the squeeze. Often to get the flow that I want to use I just resort to hacking apart the Api bit by bit and making my own horrible layer on-top of the existing solution because i am still standardized but I don't have to deal with politics in making a change request. reply jzig 15 hours ago | root | parent | prev | next [–] Sage advice here, thank you. That makes a lot of sense in terms of learning the domain. Would you be comfortable having a brief conversation? Would love to learn more of your story. reply golddust-gecko 13 hours ago | parent | prev | next [–] This is great. And I think if "software engineer" as a large-scale job category (i.e. not just highly specialized big co. technical staff) persists in the AI future, it looks like this: "the jack of all trades computer person working in a non-software company". reply no-trbl-2-u 1 day ago | parent | prev | next [–] This is so sick, great job dude! I actually just started a startup with a few friends of mine and we just started using Google ads and we literally just complained about the dashboard and what we can and can not see. Probably the most interesting thing about it at the moment is the editor. The world, and most things in it, are represented as collections of SDFs. More accurately, they're density fields, but, potato-tomato. One neat thing about representing the world as SDFs is they've been thoroughly researched and documented by a guy named Inigo Quilez, and they have a lot of nice mathematical properties. For example, you can do a smooth union of arbitrary SDFs to get nice rounded contours where shapes join. The world generator and editor operate almost entirely on the GPU. The terrain and editor pipeline is a three stage process. The first stage is user-configurable; users write an arbitrary 'shaping' shader in GLSL. The second stage is a fused stage; it does a convolution on the output of the first stage to compute a normal, runs a second user-configurable 'decoration' function, and finally applies edits. Edits are collections of SDFs that are 'compiled' from a graph structure on the CPU into a bytecode, and interpreted in the shader. The last stage runs another convolution to compute the final normal, then packs an occupancy bit, color, and normal down into a 32-bit representation, suitable for transfer back to the CPU. I expect I will expand this to include additional user-level bits for encoding biome type and GPU-driven spawning. The entire shader pipeline is one fused 'ubershader' .. everything is bound at startup and the shader is dispatched three times, incrementing a 'Stage' uniform on each dispatch. This strategy conceptually makes the driver overhead nearly zero, and the profile agrees. The final step in the process is giving the CPU a chance to spawn additional entities and structures after generation. This is not completely fleshed out, but the bones are there. The idea is that the results of the GPU work are passed back to the CPU, which can run arbitrary callbacks to spawn additional edits and entities. Once spawning is complete, the result is meshed using a fast binary meshing algorithm and uploaded to the GPU. I keep 16 bits of data per voxel from the GPU work, 1 bit of occupancy, and 15 bits of normal for collision response, which works out to half a megabyte per chunk. At the moment I only keep chunks which contain a piece of the world surface, and discard the rest. Surface chunks are dense, and may be compressed in the future, but keeping this amount of data scales to world sizes greater than 1B voxels cubed, which seems good enough for now. In terms of raw performance, GPUs are ridiculous. My 3080ti mobile gets somewhere on the order of 500B-1T perlin samples per second with a naive perlin implementation. Compared to FastNoise2, that's about 1000x more, which sounds wrong since my GPU only has 35x more capacity, but, that's what my initial profiling said. That number is the marketing number; the real throughput is significantly less due to multi-stage nature of the system, but, there's a lot of headroom for improvement. For example, dropping the backing textures from 32bit to 16bit roughly quadruples performance. Since we only really care about the surface where values are near zero, I believe using 8 or 16 bit is a viable option, though this claim will require a fair amount of study to validate.
