Sign in they couldn’t have had a B8 Uranium cubes reveal why the German nuclear project failed “Our calculations suggest Heisenberg significantly underestimated the materials required.” Jennifer Ouellette – Nov 4, 2026 4:56 pm | 125 ... ... ... One of 664 uranium cubes from the failed nuclear reactor that German scientists tried to build in Haigerloch during World War II. Credit: ohn T. Consoli, University of Maryland College Park One of 664 uranium cubes from the failed nuclear reactor that German scientists tried to build in Haigerloch during World War II. Credit: ohn T. Consoli, University of Maryland College Park Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav During World War II, physicists on the Manhattan Project worried that the Nazi German nuclear program might achieve the first nuclear bomb before the US and its allies. That’s not what transpired, but historians have debated just how close the Germans came to achieving criticality in their last attempt at building a reactor: the B8 pile. Werner Heisenberg, who led that effort, claimed that they were close and had only needed a little more uranium. But according to a paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences Nexus, that was not the case: The project simply didn’t have sufficient uranium and heavy water to build a working bomb, given the design they were using. This particular research started in 2013, when University of Maryland physicist Timothy Koeth—a co-author on the new paper—received the gift of a mysterious heavy metal cube from a friend. He instantly recognized it as one of the uranium cubes used by German scientists in their unsuccessful attempt to build a working nuclear reactor. Only 14 such cubes are known to exist today. In 2019, we reported on Koeth’s quest to track down the cube’s origins, as well as several other similar cubes that had somehow found their way across the Atlantic. At the time, Koeth and his partner in the quest, then-graduate student Miriam “Mimi” Hiebert, had tracked down 10 such cubes around the US. For instance, the Smithsonian Institute had a German uranium cube in storage. They tracked a third cube to Harvard University, where it was regularly passed around to students in introductory physics classes as a curiosity. Underpinning the Manhattan Project in the US was the fear that German scientists under Adolf Hitler’s Nazi regime would beat the Allies to a nuclear bomb. The Germans had a two-year head start , but according to Koeth, “fierce competition over finite resources, bitter interpersonal rivalries, and ineffectual scientific management” resulted in significant delays in their progress toward achieving a sustained nuclear reaction. German nuclear scientists were separated into three isolated groups based in Berlin (B), Gottow (G), and Leipzig (L). Heisenberg headed the Berlin group, and as the Allied forces advanced in the winter of 1944, Heisenberg moved his team to a cave under a castle in a small town called Haigerloch—now the site of the Atomkeller Museum . That’s where the group built the B8 reactor. It resembled an “ominous chandelier,” per Koeth, because it was composed of 664 uranium cubes strung together with aircraft cable and then submerged in a tank of heavy water shielded by graphite to prevent radiation exposure. A replica of the failed B8 reactor on display at the Atomkeller Museum in Haigerloch, Germany Credit: ArtMechanic/CC BY-SA 3.0 A replica of the failed B8 reactor on display at the Atomkeller Museum in Haigerloch, Germany Credit: ArtMechanic/CC BY-SA 3.0 As the German scientists were racing against time, Manhattan Project lead Lieutenant General Leslie Groves kicked off a covert mission dubbed “Alsos,” with the express purpose of gathering information and materials related to Germany’s scientific research. When Allied forces closed in, Heisenberg took apart the B8 experiment and buried the uranium cubes in a field, ferreting away key documentation in a latrine. (Pity Samuel Goudsmit , the poor physicist who had to dig those out.) Heisenberg escaped by bicycle, carrying a few cubes in a backpack. A critical reassessment As Heisenberg reported, the German scientists’ final experiment failed because the amount of uranium in the cubes was insufficient to trigger a sustained nuclear reaction. But Heisenberg was confident that “a slight increase in its size would have been sufficient to start off the process of energy production.” A model described in a 2009 paper supported that, showing the group would have needed only 50 percent more uranium cubes to make the design work. Koeth and Hiebert uncovered a box of declassified documents about German uranium in the National Archives and found about 400 other uranium cubes from a separate reactor experiment by the Gottow group. They concluded that the combined inventory would have been more than enough to achieve criticality in the B8 reactor, suggesting that Germany’s secretive, isolationist approach hampered their nuclear program, because the two groups weren’t sharing information or resources. This latest paper builds on that earlier work but reaches a different conclusion. Koeth, Hiebert, and their co-authors analyzed two of the surviving uranium cubes, along with combing through historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and similar archival sources to learn more about the uranium, heavy water, and graphite blocks used for the B8 reactor experiment. Among their findings: The B8 reactor would have needed between 1,292 and 1,775 uranium cubes to achieve criticality, and twice the heavy water produced by the Norsk Hydro plant in Vemork, Norway—the only source at the time—over the course of the entire war. In short, “Our calculations suggest Heisenberg significantly underestimated the materials required,” the authors wrote. The authors also cited prior work noting key differences in American and German graphite production. The former used petroleum coke. While some of this supply reached Germany, the British naval blockade in January 1940 deprived the Germans of that vital resource. The German nuclear physicists had to use metallurgical coke from the Ruhr, which had twice as many impurities as American coke. (The US scientists had similar issues until they located an unusually low-boron coke in Pennsylvania.) Thus, “no natural uranium, graphite-moderated pile could have gone critical” with the materials available to the German scientists at the time. PNAS Nexus, 2026. title: RIP, Harvest
How I'm fighting the AI brain fry
body_text: How I'm fighting the AI Brain Fry — Sergey Kuhne Sergey Kuhne Blog Tools How I'm fighting the AI Brain Fry November 8, 2026 If you work with Claude Code or Codex from the terminal, you know this one. You start a task. The AI takes time to reply, so you start another one. Then the first one replies, but the reply needs one clarification, one follow up and one side task — and each of them wants its own tab. Then the second tab's reply comes in. You juggle. And all of a sudden you find yourself hopping between 20 threads, trying to keep all those contexts in your brain RAM. Until you can't. Your brain gets exhausted, your focus smashes, and you don't know anymore what you were doing, where you started, and where you were supposed to finish. A lot of people are suggesting taking breaks, thinking before typing, limiting scope. I have my own experiment. I decided this way of working has two major problems: sequencing and context. So I organised my work a bit like a priority queue. Here is how it actually works. The queue lives in git. Every ticket is a markdown file in the repo, right next to the code it talks about, and the state of the board is a committed snapshot. Nothing important lives in a chat window and nothing lives in my head. If a session dies, the queue is still there. An agent works that board in cycles. It researches new tickets, builds the ones a human has tagged as safe to build, runs the tests and a browser check, and verifies what is already deployed. For anything touching sensitive code it builds on a branch and asks first. It never deploys to production — that part is mine. What it cannot do is decide. So everything that needs me lands in one place I call my owner inbox. A script reads the whole board and hands me a prioritised list of exactly the items waiting on my judgement — review this change, answer this question, rule on this tradeoff. The reading surface is a Claude artifact. One page, rebuilt from git on every cycle, mirroring the whole board plus a review page per ticket. So I don't scroll back through a terminal trying to reconstruct what a change does. I open one link, read what was built and why, and give my verdict. The verdict goes back into git, onto the card. The page is only a viewer — git is the record. Then comes the part that matters most. I take one item. I load its context. I make a decision or request an action. And I close it, by putting it back into the queue. That closing is the whole trick. The ticket doesn't keep hanging in my memory as a thing to remember about. The context closes with it. So when I pick the next item from the queue, I can actually focus. One thing at a time. It is still exhausting. But I don't feel distracted or lost. The challenge was, and still is, the tooling around it. Getting the context served up in a digestible manner, so loading a ticket takes a minute and not twenty. And keeping tickets from going into endless loops because they are blocked waiting for a ruling only I can give. It's a living organism and I keep improving it. But it felt like a huge step forward in my productivity with AI tools, so I thought it was worth sharing. Get new posts by email One email when I publish something new. Nothing else. In 2026, attackers broke into internet-facing refrigeration supervisors across Europe using default passwords and old, unpatched firmware, then forced defrost cycles. coldframe pretends to be one of those controllers. It records who connects, what passwords they try and which public exploits they use, and it never gives them anything real. It is one Python file with no dependencies outside the standard library. Personas Persona Pretends to be What it serves danfoss Danfoss AK-SM 800A system manager StoreView login, a fake store dashboard, the XML API at /html/xml.cgi and /xml.cgi , HTTP and HTTPS dixell Copeland/Dixell XWEB EVO supervisor Login page and the XWEB 500 CGI paths targeted by public exploits Looking like a real unit The Danfoss persona copies what internet scanners record for real AK-SM 800A units: the nginx server header and header order, the Danfoss StoreView page title, TLS 1.2 only, and a 1-year certificate for CN=DanfossSM800A issued by a SelfSigned-DanfossSM800A authority. Each build generates its own keys. Weak logins (for example Supervisor / 12345 ) and a correct CVE-2025-41450 "code of the day" succeed . The attacker gets a session token and a dashboard of fake refrigerated cases with defrost buttons. Every action they take is logged as a control event; nothing is real. The Dixell persona follows real XWEB EVO units the same way: no Server header, their security-header set and order, the same asset paths and page size. Its login uses the real /cgi-bin/login.lua flow: the documented factory login Admin / Admin succeeds, five failures in five minutes lock the user, and attempts at the XWEB Pro auth_mode bypass (CVE-2026-25085) are tagged. Real units of both vendors serve their own favicon, and scanners match devices by its hash. That icon is the vendor's artwork, so it is not in this repository. For a private deployment you can point FAVICON_FILE at a copy you have the right to use. The same goes for the Danfoss start page. Real units serve a short Angular loader page from the firmware, and thousands share its exact hash. Point INDEX_FILE at that index.html (from the public firmware package) and the decoy serves it byte for byte, with its original date in Last-Modified and ETag . The loader's main.*.js then shows the decoy's own login page, laid out like the firmware's remote login. If the firmware's assets/images/Danfoss-logo.png sits beside that index.html , the page uses it. Both personas can also run an optional Modbus TCP service with fake case temperatures, setpoints and a defrost register. Real AK-SM 800A units only use Modbus to talk to their own case controllers, so Modbus is off by default. Turn it on to catch generic industrial scanners. Exploits it recognises Requests that match a public exploit get an exploit field in the log: CVE-2023-25914 : AK-SM 800A path traversal via get_file CVE-2023-25915 : AK-SM 800A command injection via load_cert CVE-2025-41452 : AK-SM 800A nginx header overwrite via load_nginx_headers CVE-2025-41450 : AK-SM 800A "code of the day" login bypass ( getauth with eds_only or quantum_only ), noting whether the attacker computed the correct code SM800 code-of-the-day bypass : eds_only / quantum_only on other commands CVE-2021-45420 : XWEB 500 upload and command paths under /cgi-bin/ CVE-2026-25085 : XWEB Pro login bypass via an unexpected auth_mode Quick start PERSONA=danfoss HTTP_PORT=8080 python3 -I honeypot.py Open http://localhost:8080 and every request shows up as a JSON line on stdout and in events.jsonl . Run the tests (they start the honeypot on loopback and attack it): python3 -I test_honeypot.py Deploying Quickest: paste into "User data" Create an Ubuntu 24.04 server (a $4 DigitalOcean droplet is plenty) and paste cloud-init.yaml into the User data box. Change PERSONA=danfoss to dixell if you want the XWEB persona. About two minutes after boot the decoy is listening on port 80 (and 443 for Danfoss), hardened as below. Then, in your provider's firewall, allow only the decoy's ports from anywhere and SSH from your own address. Read the log with: ssh root@ < server > ' podman logs coldframe ' By hand Build the container. Each build makes a fresh self-signed certificate, so two deployments never share one. podman build -t coldframe . Run it with rootful podman or Docker. Rootless port forwarding rewrites the source address, which makes every attacker look like the same internal IP. --userns=auto maps the container to an unused host UID range, so even the container user is nobody on the host. Podman needs a range to hand out, once per host: echo " containers:2147483647:2147483648 " | sudo tee -a /etc/subuid /etc/subgid sudo podman run -d --name coldframe --restart=always \ --read-only --cap-drop=ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges --userns=auto \ --memory 128m --pids-limit 512 --log-opt max-size=10m \ -p 80:8080 -p 443:8443 \ -v coldframe-logs:/logs:U \ -e PERSONA=danfoss \ coldframe For Modbus, add -e MODBUS_PORT=5020 -p 502:5020 . On the host, only expose the ports the persona would really have, and block outbound traffic except DNS and package updates: the decoy never needs to connect out. Keep SSH reachable only from your own address: a fridge controller with SSH open to the world looks wrong. Configuration Variable Default Meaning PERSONA danfoss danfoss or dixell HTTP_PORT 8080 HTTP listener HTTPS_PORT 0 (off) HTTPS listener, needs CERT_FILE and KEY_FILE MODBUS_PORT 0 (off) Modbus TCP listener LOG_PATH events.jsonl Where events are appended FAVICON_FILE none Optional favicon to serve (private deployments only) INDEX_FILE none Optional Danfoss firmware index.html to serve as the start page (private deployments only) Reading the log Each line is one event: { "ts" : " 2026-11-05T10:57:21.158+00:00 " , "persona" : " danfoss " , "proto" : " http " , "src_ip" : " 203.0.113.7 " , "src_port" : 6782 , "event" : " login_attempt " , "username" : " admin " , "password" : " admin " } event When request Any HTTP(S) request, with method, path, Host, User-Agent, Authorization and body login_attempt Credentials submitted through the login page or the XML API, with granted control An action from a logged-in session, such as starting a defrost xml_cmd A Danfoss XML API command, with its attributes and any exploit match tls_error A failed TLS handshake (often a scanner speaking plain HTTP to 443) connect , read , write , device_id , unsupported , malformed Modbus activity; writes to the defrost registers carry "defrost": true summary.py turns a log into a short report: python3 -I summary.py --hours 24 --ignore < your-own-ip > < events.jsonl Safety It never runs commands, reads files, or forwards traffic. Exploit payloads are logged and dropped. Request bodies, logged fields and connections are capped, including a per-source limit so one attacker cannot crowd out others. Idle sockets time out, and the event log rotates once it gets large. Connections that trickle data to stay open are cut after 30 seconds, and refused connections are logged. Over-long log lines are truncated, and summary.py neutralises terminal escape codes from attacker input. The container runs as a non-root user in its own user namespace, on a read-only filesystem with no capabilities. Log fields are attacker-controlled. Treat them as untrusted when you view or process them. Limitations Shallow interaction. Logged-in attackers see a small dashboard and a handful of XML commands, not the full StoreView app. Public code can be fingerprinted. Anyone can read this repository and spot its exact responses. Change the persona strings, page layout and certificate subject for your deployment. Unconfirmed details. Static paths, the full web app and some XML response shapes of real units are not public. Where they were missing, coldframe uses plausible values. Cloud IPs look suspicious. Some scanners flag industrial devices on cloud hosting as likely honeypots. Sources Danfoss AK-SM 800A user guide (port table, login screen, StoreView Web): https://assets.danfoss.com/documents/latest/590332/BC337629891709en-001101.pdf Danfoss AK-SM XML interface guide: https://assets.danfoss.com/documents/latest/376199/AU342138209420en-000501.pdf Synacktiv, AK-SM 800A vulnerabilities (CVE-2023-25914, CVE-2023-25915): https://www.synacktiv.com/sites/default/files/2023-10/synacktiv-danfoss-sm800a-multiple-vulnerabilities.pdf Synacktiv, SM800 auth bypass: https://www.synacktiv.com/sites/default/files/2023-10/synacktiv-danfoss-sm800-sc255-sc355-auth-bypass.pdf Claroty Team82, Danfoss controller research (CVE-2025-41450 to 41452): https://blog.claroty.com/team82/research/freeze-the-controller-defrost-the-food-uncovering-vulnerabilities-in-danfoss-refrigeration-controllers Exploit-DB 50639, XWEB 500 (CVE-2021-45420): https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/50639 Copeland XWEB EVO operation manual r5.4.1 (default login, lockout): https://webapps.copeland.com/Dixell/Content/Pages/Manuals/XWEBEVO/XWEBEVOV5.4.1OPERATION/XWEB-EVO-r5.4.1-OPR-EN.pdf CISA ICSA-26-057-10 and Claroty Team82, XWEB Pro vulnerabilities: https://claroty.com/team82/research/chilling-discoveries-unpacking-vulnerabilities-in-copeland-xweb-pro-controllers Ironhackers, CVE-2025-41450 code-of-the-day analysis: https://ironhackers.es/en/danfoss-ak-sm-800a-cve-2025-41450/ Shodan records of exposed units (header set, title, certificate fields), November 2026 Related work eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy is another AK-SM decoy, with SNMP and Service Tool listeners and a richer simulated store. coldframe focuses on matching real units' web fingerprints, detecting specific exploits, and Dixell XWEB support. 256K context uses 432 MB KV 64 GB Desktop / Server 64 GB DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B ( 56.56 GiB , 1.71 bpw ) 44.4 tok/s pp · 9.1–14.7 tok/s tg Fits in 62.5 GiB usable Linux RAM (57.61 GiB VmRSS) with zero NVMe swap Hybrid Desktop (CPU + 16 GB GPU) 32–64 GB Nemotron-30B / Qwen3-30B ( 3.75–4.25 bpw ) 80.80 tok/s Hot attention/SSM trunk on GPU ( -ngl 99 ), cold routed MoE experts in CPU RAM 8-Channel Workstation (Threadripper) 128 GB+ DeepSeek-284B / Nemotron-30B 111.62 tok/s (30B) 8-CCD AVX-512BW _1x8 register tiling saturates 8-channel DDR5 bandwidth Overview llama-modchip is a set of ggml / llama.cpp kernel patches, quantization transcoders, and runtime tools designed to run sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) checkpoints entirely in system RAM on x86_64 ( AVX-512 / AVX2 ) and ARM64 ( NEON / SVE / Apple Metal) processors: Fitting 284B DeepSeek-V4-Flash into 64 GB Physical RAM ( 56.56 GiB on disk, 1.71 bpw ): Standard UD-IQ1_S builds of DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( 284.33B total, 13.17B active across 43 MLA layers and 256 routed experts) occupy 76.87 GiB ( 82.5 GB ), exceeding the ~62.5 GiB of usable RAM on a 64 GB Linux system and causing page-cache thrashing or OOM kills. llama-modchip reduces the checkpoint to 56.56 GiB ( 60.73 GB ) so the entire model plus a 256K KV cache ( 57.61–58.9 GiB VmRSS ) locks into RAM with zero swap. By default, all 6 routed experts per layer ( Top-6 ) are evaluated without pruning. CPU Cache & SIMD Kernel Patches ( +77% prefill, +53% decode): Replaces single-column quantized matrix-vector loops during prompt prefill with a 4-level register ( ZMM AVX-512BW) + L1D ( 32 KB ) + L2 ( 1 MB ) + L3 ( 64 MB ) multi-column ( {8,4,3,2} ) tiling schedule ( 25.0 -> 44.36 tok/s on 16-core Zen 5), register-stationary MQA8 FlashAttention, and non-temporal _MM_HINT_NTA MoE streaming so cold expert weights do not evict hot KV cache lines from L3. Self-Speculative Drafting & Instant Agent Context Restore: Pairs a 1.64 MB L2/L3 Zobrist n-gram drafter ( Stockfish-PVS v2 ) with /dev/shm KV slot snapshots ( 13.1–32.6 ms restore time for 40-tool Claude Code prompts) and an $O(1)$ speculative rollback fix for deepseek4 recurrent/MLA states. Quantization & Memory Breakdown To answer the most common technical question upfront— exact bit-widths ( bpw ), base checkpoints, and what is compressed in each GGUF : Checkpoint Total / Active Params Base Source Disk Size ( GiB / GB ) Effective bpw Layer-by-Layer Tensor Allocation Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Q4_0 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 17.59 GiB ( 18.89 GB ) 4.50 bpw Standard Q4_0 across MoE + attention; F32 norms & SSM conv/decay Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-MXFP4 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 15.95 GiB ( 17.13 GB ) 4.25 bpw GGML_TYPE_MXFP4 ( E2M1 + shared exponent) on routed MoE; Q4_0 / Q8_0 trunk Nemotron-3.5-30B-A3B-Fractal-64 30.2B / 3.0B BF16 Official 14.35 GiB ( 15.41 GB ) 3.75 bpw Attention, Mamba-2 SSM & shared experts in Q4_0 / Q8_0 / F32 ; cold routed MoE experts in hybrid Q4_0 + Fractal-64 ( Q2_0 , 64-weight block + BF16 scale). Scores 100/100 on benchmarks/eval_quality_and_tools.py . DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Fractal 284.33B / 13.17B Unsloth UD-IQ1_S ( 76.87 GiB / 82.5 GB ) 56.56 GiB ( 60.73 GB ) 1.71 bpw • Embeddings, Dense L0, 43 Shared Experts ( shexp ), MLA kv_a / q_a / wkv_b : Preserved in Q4_K / Q5_K / F32 • MLA wq_b & attn_output ( wo_a / wo_b ): Transcoded to Fractal-64 ( GGML_TYPE_Q2_0 , 3.75 bpw , 30B/64-block w/ 8 sub-scales & BF16 scale) • 256 Routed MoE Experts ( ffn_*_exps ): Primarily IQ1_S ( 1.5625 bpw ) with analytical SwiGLU-H2 second-order scale matching; sensitive boundary layers preserved in IQ2_XXS ( 2.06 bpw ) & IQ1_M ( 1.75 bpw ) ( -20.31 GiB vs UD-IQ1_S ). Retains 98.5 / 100 on benchmarks/eval_quality_and_tools.py ( 100% JSON tool-calling & 8.5K/256K needle accuracy, 0.9964 top-logit cosine similarity vs 76.87 GiB UD-IQ1_S ; full ablation in docs/DEEPSEEK_V4_OPTIMIZATIONS.md ). Note on MoE Expert Routing ( Top-K ): By default ( v2.4.0 Lossless ), DeepSeek-V4-Flash evaluates all 6 routed experts + 1 shared expert ( Top-6 ) per layer with zero expert dropping ( 1.00000 logit cosine similarity vs the unpatched runtime on the same checkpoint). Setting LLAMA_MOE_TOP_K=5 or 4 is an optional runtime flag for users who want to trade a small perplexity delta for higher decode throughput. title: Making any integer with four 2s (2025)
body_text: Making any integer with four 2s - Eli Bendersky's website Toggle navigation Eli Bendersky's website About Projects Archives Making any integer with four 2s February 22, 2025 at 14:53 Tags Math There's a cute math puzzle that can be interesting to folks on very different levels: Given exactly four instances of the digit 2 and some target natural number, use any mathematical operations to generate the target number with these 2s, using no other digits. Some examples can be done by elementary school kids: \[\begin{align*} 1&=\frac{2+2}{2+2}\\ 2&=\frac{2}{2}+\frac{2}{2}\\ 3&=2\cdot2-\frac{2}{2}\\ 4&=2+2+2-2\\ 5&=2\cdot 2 +\frac{2}{2}\\ 6&=2\cdot 2\cdot 2 - 2\\ \end{align*}\] In middle school, kids learn about exponents, factorials, etc. which expands the range considerably: \[\begin{align*} 18&=2^{2^{2}}+2\\ 28&=(2+2)!+2+2\\ 256&=(2+2)^{2+2}\\ 65536&=2^{2^{2^{2}}}\\ \end{align*}\] Then come the tricks; for example, the number 22 (twenty two) can be seen as a valid use of two 2s, and so on; so we can have: \[\begin{align*} 26&=22+2+2\\ 11&=\frac{22}{\sqrt{2+2}}\\ 444&=222\cdot 2\\ \end{align*}\] Getting to 7 is notoriously difficult, but if you allow even more mathematical tools like the Gamma function , it becomes easy: \[7&=\Gamma(2)+2+2+2\] The more math skill people have, the more numbers they can make. See this thread for some fun concoctions using integrals, repeating fractions and combinatorial operators. One of my favorite examples involves complex numbers: \[12=|2+2\sqrt{-2}|^2\] So the fun doesn't end even after one graduates from university! In fact, this seems to have been a favorite pastime for mathematicians in the 1920s. Until Paul Dirac ruined it for everyone by finding a general solution for every number. It's all about nested square roots: \[\begin{align*} \sqrt{2}=2^{\frac{1}{2}}=2^{2^{-1}}\\ \sqrt{\sqrt{2}}=2^{\frac{1}{4}}=2^{2^{-2}}\\ \sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{2}}}=2^{\frac{1}{8}}=2^{2^{-3}}\\ \end{align*}\] If the square root is applied n times: \[\sqrt{\sqrt{\cdots n \cdots\sqrt{2}}}=2^{2^{(-n)}}\] All that's left now is some base-2 logarithms: \[log_{2}2^{2^{(-n)}}=2^{(-n)}\] And another: \[log_{2}(log_{2}2^{2^{(-n)}})=-n\] This leads to the general formula: \[n = -log_{2}\left(log_{2}\left(\sqrt{\sqrt{\cdots n \cdots\sqrt{2}}}\right)\right)\] There's just one small wrinkle: it uses three instances of the digit 2, not four. This is easy to amend, however; since 2=\sqrt{2+2} , we can replace any single digit with that and get exactly four: \[n = -log_{\sqrt{2+2}}\left(log_{2}\left(\sqrt{\sqrt{\cdots n \cdots\sqrt{2}}}\right)\right)\] One may claim this is cheating, but it seems to be in line with the rules of the puzzle! Note that the entity n doesn't actually appear anywhere - it's just a helper to count the number of repeated square roots. For example, another way to express 7 is: \[7=-log_{\sqrt{2+2}}\left(log_{2}\left( \sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{\sqrt{2}}}}}}}\right)\right)\] There are exactly four 2s, and this uses only reasonable, elemental math operations to do the calculation. It's clear that any number can be expressed this way; the only challenge is properly drawing all those square roots! Credits I've read about this story in Graham Farmelo's book The Strangest Man: The Hidden Life of Paul Dirac, Quantum Genius . I'm enjoying this book so far. For comments, please send me an email . © 2003-2026 Eli Bendersky Back to top

title: Goodbye Claude, hello Pi
body_text: Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi caleb.software Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi 21 September 2026 #pi #claude Iâve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. Iâm certain that in a few years weâll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development weâre in. Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, Iâve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use Pi instead. Someone at Anthropic mustâve caught windâ¦ just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would finally start supporting AGENTS.md files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late. Complaining In lieu of a proper obituary, Iâd like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what Iâm looking forward to avoiding with Pi). The AGENTS.md thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Donât get me wrong, having a ton of CLAUDE.md files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats. Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review. Except you can only have one session âconnectedâ to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it canât receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at least as far back as December 2025 â¦ and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug. 1 Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands donât work at all in the GUI. It doesnât have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on. In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. Dynamic workflows , agent teams , ultrareviews â all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need. Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been 244 releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions). And what are all those changes for? Despite chopping 80% of the system prompt , Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash toolâs description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub. 2 The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way. 3 Looking Forward This post has been a lot of hating. Iâm sorry! Thatâs not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. Iâm also not under any delusion that I wouldâve done a better job if I were the one in charge of running Claude Code from the beginning. LLM coding harnesses are a very new space and being one of the first to innovate in a field is a really hard task. Later tools like Pi have the benefit of hindsight to see what works and what doesnât, whatâs a core feature and what can be cut. Ultimately, CC feels like a product without a strong vision or direction. Itâs as if a bunch of excited engineers and PMs are rapidly tacking on whatever features suit their workflowâ¦ but without consideration for how this might make things worse for other users. It seems like there isnât someone high-up whose job is strictly to say ânoâ to these requests, which is incredibly important when it comes to product engineering. So, for now, Iâm leaving. Iâm excited to lean more into Pi. The first few days required some finagling, but since then itâs been smooth sailing. Iâm enjoying the stability, minimalist approach, and the extreme level of customizability. Iâve already written a couple of extensions to support my use cases, which Iâm hoping to share soon after Iâve cleaned them up a bit. If youâre also feeling these frustrations, Iâd highly encourage giving an open source harness a try! Itâs not like thereâs some huge technical roadblock to this either. After installing Pi, I wrote an extension to handle this very functionality across multiple open tabs in like 20 minutes.Â (return) Bonus points for the fact that it instructs the model to use cat <<'EOF' which (prior to widespread rollout of auto mode) would always trip the manual review rules regardless of existing git command allowlists.Â (return) If you assume 1 million DAU and 100M requests per day, trimming 1,000 tokens off of this could literally save millions of dollars in inference costs per year. Surely thatâs worth some engineerâs time??Â (return) Thanks for Reading! I love hearing people's thoughts, so please don't hesitate to shoot me an email at calebdotsoftware@gmail.com . If you'd like to get updates whenever I publish a new post, you can subscribe over email or with RSS . If you want to comment or read the public discussion about this post, I've shared it on the following sites: Twitter , Mastodon , Bluesky Created 21 Sep 2026 · Updated 07 Nov 2026 · Build 2f1e49

title: We know 15k websites are infected. how do we tell them?
body_text: We Know 15,579 Websites Are Infected. How Do We Tell Them? Home Speaking Training Media Contact Sponsor 🌙 Subscribe Sponsored by:   Report URI - SuperPixel: a card skimmer hiding inside 100+ shops' own copy of jQuery. Would you have spotted it? Threat Intelligence We Know 15,579 Websites Are Infected. How Do We Tell Them? Scott Helme Security researcher, entrepreneur and international speaker who specialises in web technologies. More posts by Scott Helme. Scott Helme 6 Nov 2026 • 6 min read We've identified 15,579 websites that are currently infected with malicious JavaScript and between them, we conservatively estimate that they receive more than 135 million visits every month. We know they're infected, and we have the evidence to back that up, but there's a problem: how on Earth do we tell them all? As our Threat Intelligence capabilities at Report URI have grown, identifying compromised websites has become increasingly efficient. Unfortunately, responsible disclosure hasn't kept pace, and we're now finding infections considerably faster than we could ever hope to notify the affected organisations. I genuinely don't know how to solve this problem, so I'm asking for help. What attacks we're finding At the core of it, we're finding websites that are running JavaScript that they should absolutely not be running! For some examples of how nasty this can be: Credit card skimmers - often known as ' Magecart ', they target payment pages and skim full card details to send them to the attacker. ClickFix attacks - designed to trick users into completing a "prove you're human" challenge and instead installing malware on their device. Device exploitation - loading malware to compromise specific versions of iOS and install spyware, like DarkSword or Coruna . Redirects - these can send the visitor anywhere, including fake login pages to phish details, device security 'warnings', scams, and much more. All of these are bad scenarios for the innocent visitor, and attackers change their payloads depending on their objective. How these sites are compromised There are many ways an attacker can get malicious JS onto a site, but here are the main categories that we group the initial vectors into from what we're seeing: Direct compromise - typically a WordPress vulnerability or similar, the site's own JS files are modified to include the malicious JS. Supply chain - a third-party script file that a site loads is infected with malware, and is then loaded on to the site, exposing all visitors. XSS - good old traditional XSS, a vulnerability in the site itself that allows JS to be injected. DeadTag - a threat group we named recently, buying expired domains that sites still load JS from, reviving them, and serving malware. Unfortunately, there are a lot of different ways that this can go wrong, as we're seeing. The scale of the problem Right now, we have 15,579 unique sites that are infected with one of the malicious JS attacks listed above. Those are the sites where there is no doubt in our mind, and the list of sites where we have some suspicion but haven't got to 100% confidence is thousands more. Take September as an example, because we haven't quite finished processing everything from October yet, and this is the tally for new sites that we identified as being infected: These are the sites that, as of today, are still infected. We remove sites once they clear their own infection as we have no concern about trying to notify them, so there were more than this. In terms of traffic volumes, it's quite surprising how quickly this adds up. None of the sites in the list are global leaders, but we do have a huge presence of regional leaders. For example, if we look at .fr , .es and .de sites, some of them are really highly ranked sites in those countries, but they barely crack the Top 1 Million globally. Being a top site in France still gets you quite a hefty amount of traffic it turns out. Using various sources of data, and being ultra-conservative with our estimates, our list of currently infected sites is comfortably receiving a combined 135 million visits a month. That's a lot of exposure. So, what do we do? We continue to reach out directly to those sites that we identify as particularly high impact and try to notify them, though this is happening on an admittedly small scale. The process of responsible disclosure consumes a lot of resources, use of security.txt is low, and the vast majority of our emails and messages go unanswered. It's simply not possible for us to scale this up. As these are sites we're crawling and identifying ourselves, we have no contact information like we would for a customer. So, as things currently stand, that's where we are, and I'd like to hear suggestions on what we can do. If you're from an NCSC/CERT, especially in Europe where we seem to be finding a lot of impacted sites, please reach out to intel@report-uri.com and we'd be happy to provide a list of infected sites in your region. Hopefully you would be able to have more success in notifying the impacted sites than we would. If you're an organisation and believe having commercial access to our threat intelligence feeds would help you protect your own customers, you can also reach out to intel@report-uri.com for details. Back to the original problem, though, and it pains me to say it but I don't have a clear idea on how we can try to have more of a positive impact. If you think there's something you can help with, an idea you'd like to put forward, or a suggestion on what we can do with all of this data, please drop by the comments below and I'd be happy to hear from you. We have intelligence that could help protect millions of website visits, and we need help to turn it into action. Update: 6th Nov 2026 21:36 UTC A lot of questions have been raised across various social channels and especially the HN thread , so I thought I'd answer them in one central place: Why hasn't the list of sites been published? There are a few reasons: I didn't want this to be a 'name and shame' as the sites on that list are, after all, victims of attacks. Someone broke into their site, and the owners probably have no idea. If the list is widely disseminated and absorbed into blocklists, trying to get your domain of those lists afterwards is close to impossible. For a small business, that could be devastating. Many of these websites were likely infected because of an existing vulnerability that was exploited in something like WordPress, Magento or similar. Handing out a list of viable targets does not seem like a good idea. Why not use the WHOIS contacts? Since GDPR back in 2018, I've found that data to be mostly useless. What you get is either nothing, a registrar web form, or a relay address such as the Namecheap or GoDaddy privacy mailboxes. Why not contact the hosting providers? Because so many of these sites are behind a CDN provider or other proxy service, so the IP resolution doesn't give any indication of who the hosting provider is to contact them. Why not just send an email to every website? I could probably try to automate that, but to what email address? I'd have to hit a selection of common ones, info@, support@, abuse@, maybe others? There are also close to 16,000 of them, have you ever tried to send 16,000 emails? The manually curated emails have almost no response rate so a spammy mailshot seems unlikely to help, and could also trash my email reputation! Update: 9th Nov 2026 12:03 UTC We'll start with the good news that multiple NCSCs/CERTs have reached out and have been provided with the data, and warnings are being sent out starting today from some of those organisations! As an example, NCSC UK has their Early Warning system where domain owners can request to be notified about intelligence relating to their infrastructure. These ongoing efforts currently cover the UK (NCSC) and EU (ENISA), with some regional EU CSIRTs involved, and we have contacted CISA (USA). The bad news is that, inevitably, we have now passed through a confirmed 16,000 sites infected. The current total stands at 16,068 sites , an addition of 489 infected sites since publishing this blog post on Friday, 3 days ago. In addition, 3 of those sites were considered quite high value and we've made efforts to contact them directly. One of those sites almost makes it into the Top 10K sites in the World, with a rank of ~12,500 according to Tranco . title: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab
body_text: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab | Bosscher before the browser paints. Runs synchronously, no defer/async. --> Skip to content Bosscher Posts Tags About Archives Search Go back What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab 7 Nov, 2026 | Edit page A while ago I bought an OpenStick on a whim for 10 dollars (including shipping!) because it seemed like such a cool novelty piece of hardware. For 10 dollars you get: 512 MB of RAM (~450 MB usable) 4x ARM Cortex-A53 CPU cores at 1 GHz 4 GB eMMC flash 150 Mbit/s Wi-Fi 4G modem and GPS Passively cooled, so 100% silent! 1 programmable LED :) Now, you might look at this hardware and think âmy watch is more powerful than thatâ, and you wouldnât necessarily be wrong, but thereâs still a lot of fun to be had with a device this size, and itâs a great gadget to get started with self-hosting. The installation process is a bit involved, but once youâre up and running it runs Debian, which brings all the classic goodies such as systemd (among other things, a scheduler and service monitoring for Linux) and Podman (lightweight containerization). For 10 USD you basically get a home server with minimal power usage and zero noise! Thereâs actually a lot of useful software that runs great on this thing. Some of my favorites are: CastSponsorSkip (5â10 MB) This is a little service that connects to any running Google Cast device and skips sponsorships (and sometimes ads). It barely uses any resources, and after a while you forget that it exists, but it does make the whole YouTube experience a lot nicer! CastSponsorSkip AdGuard Home - my own fork (40 MB) AdGuard Home blocks bad domains at the DNS level: spyware, malware, and so on. These days devices have a tendency to spy on you. Smart TVs run content recognition continuously, washing machines scan your network, and your coffee maker might be spying on you. A DNS blocker cannot block all bad requests (youâll need a proper firewall for that), but it sure can block a whole lot. After adding a few blocklists, 60% of my queries are now blocked. Most seem harmless, but Iâm pretty sure that some arenât. Iâm running my own fork, which can handle large blocklists in an efficient manner, but you probably shouldnât run binaries provided by random strangers, so Iâve also included the link to the official version below (which is totally fine if you limit yourself to smaller blocklists). AdGuard Home Next-Gen - 40 MB (independent of the size of the blocklist) AdGuard Home - 40 MB (with a small (200k) blocklist) Zeroclaw (64 MB) Zeroclaw is an AI agent harness. It supports 30 channels (Telegram, email, WhatsApp, etc.), has sensible security defaults, a nice web UI, and integrations with all the major LLM providers. I ran OpenClaw for a while on my Kubernetes cluster, but it mostly caused a lot of frustration: it worked, but it used 1 GB+ of memory, broke with every update, and they kept changing functionality in ways that broke my existing workflows. Zeroclaw feels like a breath of fresh air. It uses ~3 MB RSS when idle, covers all the functionality that I need, and the security defaults are sensible and easy enough to disable. The next version will (hopefully!) have rich message support for Telegram, implemented by yours truly. The PR can be tracked here! Iâve given Zeroclaw access to the OpenStick (but nothing beyond that). Effectively itâs a root shell, but given that the blast radius is limited, I figured it would be acceptable. I mostly use this to monitor the OpenStick, with questions such as âanything in the logs that requires my attention?â or âhow is the disk space?â. The biggest advantage is that it communicates through Telegram, so if Iâm in the mountains with limited signal, I can still ask it how my little server is doing :) I looked at alternatives such as Picoclaw and Nullclaw, and no doubt theyâre good as well. However, Zeroclaw seemed to have the best documentation and the most active community, so I went with that :) GitHub Zeroclaw Documentation Cloudflare Tunnel (~8-20 MB) Cloudflared makes it possible to expose all these services securely to the big, bad internet, for free, without exposing any ports. The downside might be that the NSA might be able to read everything you do, but for a homelab I consider that to be an acceptable trade-off. Cloudflare Tunnel Beszel (20 MB) Beszel shows a pretty graph of memory, CPU usage, and so on, and alerts you if something looks suspicious, all while using very little memory. I ran Grafana and the whole stack on my Kubernetes cluster for a while, and itâs powerful, but not extremely user friendly, and it felt like overkill. Beszel is a really awesome solution: it looks pretty and requires ~20 MB, 10 MB for the agent and 10 MB for the server. It has built-in alerting for a whole bunch of protocols, and I let it send messages to Telegram when something requires my attention. GitHub Beszel Dozzle Dozzle is a pretty interface for managing Podman containers. It has a large overlap with Beszel, so if I ever need to save 10 or 20 MB, Iâll get rid of one of them. Dozzle has a way better interface for checking Podman logs, but it doesnât offer the same level of stats as Beszel does. GitHub Dozzle Gatus (10 MB) Beszel monitors your server(s). Gatus monitors your services. In other words, if you would like to get a notification when your webserver or database has crashed, youâll want Gatus. It also creates a really pretty web interface! GitHub Gatus - 10 MB Fusion RSS (22 MB) RIP Google Reader . I tried Feedly for a while, but 7 USD for the Pro version was just a little bit more than I felt comfortable with. Besides, why pay when you can have hours of fun setting up your own alternative? I tried a whole bunch of RSS readers and eventually settled on Fusion. It does all I need, looks good, feels responsive, and uses 22 MB of RAM. GitHub Fusion - 22 MB Shiori (~10â20 MB) Browser bookmarks are great, however a lot of my older bookmarks have stopped working because the sites disappeared, the URLs changed, or for a myriad of other reasons. Shiori fixes this by offering a great bookmark manager that also automatically archives the website. It does so in ~10 MB. You can expect some spikes when archiving, but nothing that our mighty OpenStick cannot handle! Shiori - 10 MB Diun (9 MB) Just a little service that sends a message to my Telegram whenever one of my containers has an update available. title: The $8 Linux Computer (2022)
body_text: The Little Engineer That Could: The $8 linux computer (part 1.) The Little Engineer That Could As a one man game studio (an INDIEvidual) Bram Stolk develops games. This is his development diary. Thursday, December 15, 2022 The $8 linux computer (part 1.) Yes, you read that right... for $8 you can run linux on a RISC-V computer. And not just a stripped down kernel without an MMU. No, the Ox64 comes with capable RISC-V cores. Heck, and not just one core, but three cores (all different.) Exciting times! Caveat Emptor! At the time of writing, ethernet, wifi and SD-Card are not working. It's good to realize this before jumping into this. It looks like a microcontroller, but behaves like a UNIX machine. Sweet, or what? Getting it up and running, though, is far from trivial. There are so many hurdles to take! Hurdle 1 : You cannot program it using USB, like you would an Arduino, ESP32, Stamp-C3 or rPi Pico. Nope... this needs to be programmed via the UART TX/RX pins. In the picture above, you can see them hooked up to GPIO14 / GPIO15 and GND. Hudle 2 : The flashing tool Dev Cube will crash on launch when using Ubuntu on Wayland: you have to switch to Xorg instead. $ ./BLDevCube-ubuntu Warning: Ignoring XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland on Gnome. Use QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland to run on Wayland anyway. /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/gio/modules/libdconfsettings.so: undefined symbol: g_log_structured_standard Failed to load module: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/gio/modules/libdconfsettings.so GLib-GIO-Message: Using the 'memory' GSettings backend. Your settings will not be saved or shared with other applications. (BLDevCube-ubuntu:54646): GLib-GIO-ERROR **: Settings schema 'org.gnome.settings-daemon.plugins.xsettings' does not contain a key named 'antialiasing' Trace/breakpoint trap (core dumped) So, UART programming then... fine, we'll just use one of those little CH340G dongles. I got one off Amazon, but it would not work... every time the handshake would fail in Dev Cube ( hurdle 3 ). Luckily, some people found out that you can program it with an RP2040 device, like the rPi Pico. I had a KB2040 from Adafruit lying around, so used that. Which puts us at hurdle 4 : How to turn a KB2040 into a serial bridge between PC and Ox64? Hook up GPIO-4 of the RP2040 to GPIO-15 of the Ox64. Hook up GPIO-5 of the RP2040 to GPIO-14 of the Ox64. Also, connect the grounds, of course. See below how to hook up for flashing the M0.\ Then we need to load our RP2040 with picoprobe which we can do by holding BOOT while powering up, and feeding it the uf2 file with picoprobe. Ok, so now we can flash it then? Unfortunately, no, hurdle 5 : DevCube is still not able to flash the Ox64, but we can use bflb-mcu-tool instead. Ok, but with bflb-mcu-tool, we are all set! Are we? Introducing hurdle 6 : we need to modify the tool before it will work for us. This means stripping DTR and RTS stuff from the tool by editing the ~/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/bflb_mcu_tool/libs/bflb_interface_uart.py file. Here is my copy . So with the Ox64 powered via MicroUSB, and the RP2040 connected to my PC using USB-C, I can finally flash something. For that, I took the low_load_bl808_m0.bin from the bl808 linux guide and flashed it with: $ bflb-mcu-tool --chipname=bl808 --port=/dev/ttyACM2 --baudrate=2000000 --firmware=out/low_load_bl808_m0.bin After which I now get output from my Ox64, via my KB2040 to my PC: dynamic memory init success,heap size = 156 Kbyte E907 start... mtimer clk:1000000 psram clk init ok! Ok, a modest start, but the Ox64 is talking to my PC now! Yay! Come back to my blog at a later time to see if I will manage to run Linux on the Ox64! Because as I understand it, I also need to flash something to the D0 and then flash the actual OS as well. UPDATE: Here is PART 2 . Posted by Bram at 5:49 PM Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook Share to Pinterest 3 comments: Flemming Madsen December 17, 2022 at 11:52 AM > You cannot program it using USB, like you would an Arduino, ESP32 Strictly speaking, these are not programmed via USB either, but also via RX/TX on the (debug) UART Reply Delete Replies Alan Carvalho de Assis December 23, 2022 at 5:04 AM Sorry to correct you Mr. Flemming, but you are wrong. Please download the ESP32-C3 TRM and look at chapter 29 USB_SERIAL_JTAG. This MCU has a USB IP with a CDC/ACM in the ROM, just connect the USB D+ and D- cable directly to the chip pins and you can flash it, without any external chip. Think about ARM SWD DAP connected directly to MCU's USB peripheral. I hope other vendors copy this idea from Espressif, it makes our life easier! Delete Replies Reply Reply mks February 10, 2023 at 10:24 PM Thanks very much for documenting this. title: Libghostty 1.0
body_text: Libghostty 1.0 – Mitchell Hashimoto Mitchell Hashimoto About Writing Misc Mitchell Hashimoto Libghostty 1.0 November 6, 2026 libghostty-vt 1.0 is here. libghostty is a portable, high-performance C library for terminal emulation, extracted directly from the core of Ghostty. The 1.0 release means both the library itself and the C ABI are now stable. A little over a year ago, I wrote that libghostty is coming . At the time, the Zig module had just been merged, the C API didn't exist, and nobody but Ghostty was a consumer. Today, the C API is a complete terminal emulator, it runs in production for millions of people across hundreds of products, both free and commercial, and it has a real, enforced ABI stability policy. This post is about how we got here and what 1.0 actually means. 1 Who Is Already Using It Since starting the Ghostty project in 2022, the most common question I've been asked is "why?". I already answered this in the libghostty is coming post, so feel free to read that if you wish. Today, I'd rather answer this by showing the broad industry impact libghostty has already had . I believe this strongly validates its existence. A year ago, I used a bug in JediTerm , the terminal emulator in JetBrains IDEs, as an example of why terminal emulation is hard to get right. A year later, the terminal in JetBrains IDEs now runs on libghostty . Every IntelliJ, PyCharm, GoLand, etc. user now has a libghostty-powered terminal. Based on a report by JetBrains, that's over 12.5 million active users. Neovim has an approved pull request replacing libvterm with libghostty-vt . Among other things, it closes a 10-year-old issue about reflowing scrollback on resize. The maintainers are waiting on a tagged release before merging so that distributions can package the dependency separately, and the release today should enable that. KDE developers are experimenting with a Konsole replacement built on it. Vercel's Turborepo uses it to render task output in its TUI. devenv uses it to drive shells. Antithesis used it to fuzz TUI programs and found real bugs in btop and others. Ghostel brings it to Emacs. ghostty-web is the WASM build with an Xterm.js-compatible API. Commercial products like OrbStack embed it. And a whole wave of new terminals and "agentic" coding tools, such as herdr and cmux , have been built on it rather than writing yet another emulator. There are community bindings for Rust, Go, JavaScript, Swift, Python, .NET, Elixir, Dart, Java, and more, and the awesome-libghostty list tracks well over a hundred projects. More people today use a terminal powered by libghostty than use Ghostty the application, by a very large multiple. And libghostty is having a much larger impact than being "just" a terminal emulator. 2 ABI Stability 1.0 means libghostty-vt follows semantic versioning and has strict ABI compatibility promises so that packagers across distributions and operating systems can be confident packaging libghostty-vt and program developers can be confident dynamically linking against it. Beyond providing useful features, I believe the hallmark of a high-quality and enduring C library is ABI stability. So from the start, I took inspiration from C libraries I enjoyed working with and designed the API to have a strong, stable ABI that allows for future additions. Every object is an opaque handle. The hundreds of values you might read or write go through a small set of enum-keyed getters and setters, so we can add new values easily without introducing a new symbol. Programs with newer headers linked against an older libghostty get GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED results instead of crashes or undefined behavior. The few non-opaque structs we have carry their size so that fields can be appended later, or contain reserved padding. Enums are pinned to int on every compiler, as much as the C standard allows. Our CI enforces our ABI policy. Every change is checked with libabigail against a committed baseline on Linux, and against golden type manifests on macOS and WebAssembly. On ELF platforms, every exported symbol is also versioned, so the dynamic loader refuses to load a mismatched library by name rather than failing in some mysterious way later. Packaging In addition to ABI stability, the 1.0 release brings along the proper build tooling, tarballs, dependency licensing manifests, documentation, and more to enable every major operating system and distribution to package libghostty-vt through standard official tooling. Libghostty has its own release cycle, separate from Ghostty the application. And it has its own tarballs with only the files and dependencies libghostty needs, resulting in smaller sizes and simpler licensing verification and compatibility. Each release publishes a signed source tarball along with a companion dependencies tarball containing every Zig package in Zig's own cache layout, so a distribution can build the library completely offline. The build installs the shared and static libraries with a proper SONAME, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config, and it honors --prefix , DESTDIR , and lib64 . Debug info is kept by default so distros can split it out. All of this is documented in PACKAGING-LIBGHOSTTY.md , which ships with the tarball. Dependencies and Licensing libghostty-vt is MIT licensed. At runtime it needs nothing beyond libc, and it can be built fully freestanding if you don't want that either. 3 The library compiles in a small number of permissively licensed dependencies: simdutf and Google Highway for SIMD, a compact Unicode table for grapheme data, and Wuffs for image decoding in the Kitty graphics protocol. Both simdutf and Highway are built without libc++ , so there is no C++ standard library dependency. There is no copyleft code anywhere in the dependency tree. Every dependency is listed in a machine-readable manifest with its version, SPDX license, and hash, specifically so distros can fill in their bundled-library metadata more easily. If a distro would rather dynamically link the system simdutf or Highway, there's a build flag for that. Portability libghostty-vt is highly portable. The table below lists all the platforms and architectures that we build and test (full unit tests plus running all examples) in CI: Platform Architectures Linux (glibc, musl) x86_64 , aarch64 macOS 13+ x86_64 , aarch64 iOS 13+ aarch64 FreeBSD x86_64 , aarch64 Windows x86_64 Android aarch64 , x86_64 , arm WebAssembly wasm32 (freestanding) There is a second set of platforms we build in CI but do not run tests for. These systems all have known users; we just haven't set up the machinery for automated testing: Platform Architectures Bare metal riscv32 , thumb WebAssembly (WASI) wasm32 Windows arm64 illumos x86_64 32-bit x86 x86 Each of the tested platforms gets the artifacts it expects: Linux and FreeBSD get a shared library with a proper SONAME and versioned symbols, a static library, headers, pkg-config files, and a CMake package config. macOS and iOS get a dylib with an @rpath install name and compatibility version, plus an XCFramework covering macOS, iOS, and the iOS simulator that drops straight into Xcode or Swift Package Manager. Windows gets a DLL with a .pdb , an import library, and a static library. The library is built with the GNU ABI, but MSVC programs link against it through the import library and CI verifies this. Android gets a shared library built against the NDK with 16 KB page size support, as required by Android 15+. WebAssembly ships in two flavors, one optimized for speed and one for size, and the small one is under a megabyte with every feature enabled. If you only need a read-only viewer, subsystems like input encoding, search, selection, and Kitty graphics can be compiled out with a build flag, which roughly halves the module. Every function stays exported and simply returns GHOSTTY_UNSUPPORTED so your code doesn't have to change. 4 Portability isn't just about the ability to build and run. It's also about resource usage and being able to work in a wide variety of resource environments. For resource usage, the library creates no threads, allocates only through an allocator you can customize, and uses minimal compute and memory. I've run 10,000 active terminals, each with a live shell producing output, on a Linux server with 4 cores and 8 GB of RAM. In this test, I had to use dash because bash used far more RAM than libghostty-vt and wouldn't fit into the 8 GB budget. What's Next Libghostty 1.0 is a major milestone. You can now create a terminal in ~1,500 lines of C that has more features and better performance than just about any terminal that existed in 2025, and most today in 2026. 5 And thanks to the rich ecosystem of language bindings, you can do this in every major programming language. You get this for free. For almost no effort. You can just do it. libghostty-vt is a generalized library, so we will focus on stability while implementing as many terminal protocols as exist (giving options to enable/disable them, of course) so that embedders have the luxury of choice. Every bug any libghostty-vt embedder reports makes everyone else in the ecosystem better. Every feature we ship in libghostty-vt becomes available to everyone quickly and safely. Terminals can move faster with less fragmentation. Thank you to everyone who contributed to the library, wrote bindings, filed bugs, and shipped something on top of it while the API was still experimental. As with all open source, this was the work of a large community. Docs, examples, and downloads are at lib.ghostty.org . Boo. 👻 Footnotes As usual, I hate that I have to do this for every post, but I want to note this post was completely hand-written with no AI assistance. ↩ The numbers are rough because most consumers don't report usage, but JetBrains alone reports 12.5 million recurring active users , and that's before counting everything else on the list. ↩ In the original post I wrote "not even libc!" The default build does link libc, because the SIMD paths use it and the default allocator is malloc . Turn off SIMD and the library is freestanding, which is how it runs on bare-metal RISC-V and ARM targets. ↩ The feature flags aren't WASM-specific; they work on every target. They're likely useful for things like embedded devices too. ↩ "Features" here means the set of terminal protocols and sequences understood, and "performance" means parsing throughput and memory usage, since those are the parts libghostty-vt provides. ↩ November 6, 2026 © 2026 Mitchell Hashimoto. mail twitter Twitter icon mastodon github GitHub icon linkedin LinkedIn icon

title: sshole
body_text: *sshole · sshhole.com * ss h ole so openssh on musl linux (alpine, openwrt, buildroot, yocto, and a lot of the docker images you've pulled) has had a little problem since 2016. accounts that should never take a password at all (root, your key-only deploy user, ldap users, the default user on alpine's aws and azure images) take any password longer than 256 characters. yes, any password. yes. i know. yes. 1980 the first star 1990s the password check 1990s the fine print 2012 crypt stops saying NULL 2012 the 256-byte cap 2016 bob's salt 2019 the fix for the fix 2024 ten quiet years 2026 how i ran into it 1980 the first star back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd , right next to your username. in a file everyone could read. in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon . nobody's supposed to ever log in as it. a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today 3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980 Address github.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself" 1990s how sshd checks your password ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9… . the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it and if the field is just * ? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in 1990s the fine print one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash the single unix spec · crypt() · 1997 Address pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/crypt.html pretty clear. except a lot of programs never check for NULL. they just compare whatever crypt() gives back with the stored field, hit the NULL, and crash 2012 crypt stops saying NULL so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password now guess which character they picked for that " ? " yep. the star. again. musl · b3c4cc12 · aug 2012 Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12 "reportedly." musl · b3c4cc12 · the diff Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12 "should not happen" gone, NULL gone, "*" in 2012 three weeks later then musl adds sha512 crypt. the thing is, sha512crypt gets slower the longer the password is, so someone could send one giant password and keep your server busy for a long time. so musl just caps it at 256 bytes and refuses anything longer musl · 88bf5a8a · aug 29 2012 Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=88bf5a8a twenty days after the "*" commit btw musl · crypt_sha512.c @ 88bf5a8a Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/misc/crypt_sha512.c?id=88bf5a8a KEY_MAX) return 0;" loading="lazy"> so past 256 bytes crypt fails. and when crypt fails… it says "*" . musl · crypt_sha512.c Address git.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha512.c literally in the comment the whole time 2016 sshd borrows bob's salt CVE-2016-6210. ask sshd about a user that doesn't exist and it says no instantly, cause there's nothing to hash. real users take a few ms longer. so just time it and you know who exists the fix is kinda funny. no real hash to check? sshd grabs some other account's salt and hashes your password anyway, just to waste the same amount of time. still a no, just a slower no openssh-commits · jul 2016 Address lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-July/005428.html "for invalid users." and also, it turns out, real users with a * . 2019 → 2022 the fix for the fix 2019. turns out alpine's docker images had no root password. at all. CVE-2019-5021. alpine fixes it by locking root with ! but without pam, ! also kills ssh keys. and cloud images log in with keys. 2022. alpine 3.16 switches root to * . still locked, keys work again alpine aports · fbe926af · shipped in 3.16, 2022 Address gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/commit/fbe926af.patch narrator: it did not. 2016 → 2026 ten quiet years why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a * . so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows. some people got really close though libc-alpha · debian #714219 · 2013 Address sourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*" . six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0" , and closes the bug. one character away. musl mailing list · dec 2024 Address openwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2 this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*" , same limit. nobody says "sshd" openssh-commits · 30 oct 2026 Address lists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html a security review fixes pick_salt() . the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it. nov 2026 how i ran into it i was messing around with openssh, mostly the boring parts where it talks to libc, like the password code. people don't really look at that stuff, they look at the crypto. so i built sshd every way i could think of (glibc, musl, pam, no pam, shadow, no shadow) and threw like 17,600 weird logins at it. weird hashes, broken accounts, passwords way too long oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it every build agreed on every login. except musl without pam. that one said yes to things it shouldn't tl;dr try it one debian box, one alpine box. type stuff. it all runs right here in your browser, nothing gets sent anywhere ozgun 256 × A 300 × A clear 256 1024 0 bytes debian · glibc crypt(pw, bob's salt) alice's field * alpine · musl crypt(pw, bob's salt) alice's field * are you affected? is your sshd running on musl ? (alpine, openwrt, buildroot, yocto) is it not using pam ? alpine's openssh-server doesn't by default, or maybe you set UsePAM no are password logins still on? they are by default is there an account with just * as its password? key-only users, ldap users, root on alpine and some other account with a real password? then that * account takes any password between 257 and 1024 characters on alpine's official aws and azure images that's the default alpine user, and it has passwordless doas . so it's root on debian, ubuntu, fedora or anything else with glibc? going through pam? dropbear? openbsd? you're fine what now you # update. openssh 10.6p2 fixes it. $ apk upgrade openssh # can't update yet? turn password logins off. $ echo "PasswordAuthentication no" > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf $ rc-service sshd restart did you get hacked? check. check github.com/oz9un/sshole root@your-box see a line like that? an account with no password just took a password if that's the case… i'm sorry. you got hacked. by an * sshole found by ozgun kultekin at wakefield we're hiring. wakefield.co/careers

Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters Apple Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows Aisha Down Global technology reporter Fri 6 Nov 2026 11.12 EST Last modified on Fri 6 Nov 2026 11.55 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney. But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word. New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text. So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out. Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”. The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system. The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”. But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”. In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”. The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works. The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly. Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices Read more This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect , which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes. Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year. This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied. Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.
