National News Too many men suffering in silence, national health report finds Jenny Hagan, WestCentralOnline.com | Sunday, Nov 08 2026, 12:00 PM Share: Copied! Movember Canada will continue working with the federal government to engage experts and stakeholders as the strategy takes shape. Image by Mary Taylor Article continues below advertisement ↴ Too many Canadian men and boys are facing challenges with their mental health and well-being without the support they need, according to findings from a nationwide consultation that will help shape Canada's first federal strategy dedicated to men's health. Health Minister Marjorie Michel released the government's What We Heard Report on Nov. 2, highlighting concerns raised by nearly 6,000 Canadians who participated in discussions about the health and well-being of men and boys. The findings come during Movember, a month dedicated to raising awareness about men's health, and ahead of International Men's Day on Nov. 19. The report identifies mental health, social isolation and barriers to seeking help as important issues affecting men and boys across the country. Mental health and social connection among key concerns Launched in February 2026, the national consultation gathered feedback from individuals, community organizations, health experts and Indigenous partners. Participants emphasized the importance of improving mental health services, strengthening social connections and reducing the barriers that prevent men and boys from seeking assistance. The report also highlights the role of mentorship, positive male role models, healthy relationships and community-based support programs. Health Canada says the experiences of men and boys can vary significantly depending on factors such as age, income, culture, geographic location and personal circumstances. Those differences are particularly relevant when considering access to health services in rural and remote communities, where available resources and support networks may differ from those in larger centres. "Nearly 6,000 people from across Canada took part in our national conversation on men and boys' health, sharing their observations and perspectives," Michel said. "We heard that too many men and boys are struggling, often without the support they need." The federal government says the feedback will help identify priorities for improving health outcomes and encouraging men to seek support before problems become more serious. Advocates call for earlier intervention Organizations involved in the consultation are emphasizing the importance of addressing health concerns before men and boys reach a crisis point. Kenton Boston, president and CEO of the Canadian Men's Health Foundation, said earlier intervention is essential. "For too long, we have waited until they're in crisis before offering help. We need to reach boys and young men earlier," Boston said. He added that improving the health of men and boys can have broader benefits for families and communities. Movember, which supported the federal consultation as an independent partner, also stressed the importance of social connection and preventative approaches. Andrew Little, Movember's global chief executive officer, said improving men's health requires creating conditions that support healthier lives long before serious problems develop. "The findings reinforce what we've long heard from our community: improving men's health starts well before a crisis, by strengthening social connections and creating the conditions for men and boys to live healthier, longer lives," Little said. Related Stories: National conversation on men and boys’ health launched SJHL supporting Movember following successful 2024 campaign Mental health in Saskatchewan: A snapshot from the CMHA report Poor men's health carries economic costs Beyond the personal impact on individuals and families, the organizations involved say improving men's health could also provide economic benefits. According to a 2025 study by Movember Canada, improving men's health could save the country an estimated $12.4 billion annually, with additional economic benefits possible through increased productivity. The federal government says improving men's health will complement ongoing efforts focused on women's health, recognizing that different populations face distinct challenges and may require different approaches to prevention, treatment and support. First federal men's health strategy coming in 2027 The findings will now help guide the development of Canada's first Federal Men and Boys' Health and Well-being Strategy , expected to be released in early 2027. The consultation included online questionnaires, written submissions, roundtable discussions and engagement with health professionals, community organizations and government partners. Movember Canada will continue working with the federal government to engage experts and stakeholders as the strategy takes shape. While specific programs and funding commitments have not yet been announced, the government says the goal is to develop an approach that better supports men and boys throughout their lives. With Movember underway, the findings are also drawing attention to the importance of conversations about men's mental health, encouraging help-seeking and building stronger support networks in communities across Canada. title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
body_text: The End of AI Frontiers – Machine Learning (Theory) Skip to content Machine Learning (Theory) Machine learning and learning theory research Posted on 11/6/2026 11/7/2026 by John Langford The End of AI Frontiers In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR. In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion. We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines. In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI . On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex- Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. In a scaling-only environment of course the primary effort is on getting/making/refining data, which is quite a step away from what we were working on. Aside from the incompatible focus, there was plenty of evidence that they just did not really want us. It’s a tough situation to find yourself in. I consider the scaling-only focus to be both misdirected and not fun. It is an understandable failure mode—scaling is straightforward and it’s common for people to give up on a tradeoff between multiple competing ideals (like innovation and size) by short-sightedly adopting one in totality and dropping the other. But returns to research are real and significant. For example, the Bytedance experiments suggest a variant of the Full Bandwidth Transformer might be comparable to a model of twice the size, implying significant savings in training and inference for the same capability. Do the math—how much is it worth to halve training and inference cost given that the industry has investments approaching a trillion dollars? So I situated my folks as best I could and left. I am quite fortunate in that there are many other people in the world who are capable of seeing the value of research and innovation which is my intrinsic center of interest. Every other founding AIF leadership team member seems to have come to a similar conclusion. This does leave a question: Why not go back to MSR? I chatted with folks a bit but could not get away from two serious obstacles. The first is that I am just not comfortable being at a company where the research I do has no path to real use. I could not get innovation into use (or even seriously considered) when I was in MAI, so the prospects for success from MSR seem quite small. The second is that I’m afraid there’s a breakdown of the basic deal in MSR: do good work and good things happen. As far as I can tell we did good work and were non-consensually reorged away. Unfortunately, I would not be surprised to see that kind of thing continue to happen until MSR leadership develops a will to effectively organize to meet the moment. So AI Frontiers is over. I’m sorry to say that there will not be internships with the folks there in the coming year—I enjoyed working with interns on many occasions. And my best wishes for the folks I leave behind. It is not hard to imagine a Microsoft of the future which becomes attractive for research again if the people in control can develop a little bit more wisdom. Twitter/X thread . body_text: /index.md. Do not edit: the next build overwrites it, and deploy.sh refuses to publish a generated page whose bytes do not match .build-manifest. Edit the post and re-run bin/build.py. --> Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph — Eighth Rank Skip to content the Eighth Rank Write-up Opening Played by the Bishop (Dario Pasquini) + the Knight (Michał Bazyli) 2026-10-28 Anatomy of Apple's Personal Knowledge Graph Every Mac since macOS 13 (allegedly) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph. The position A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3 , emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1 ; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. What is lost is someone else. 3r1rk1/pp2qppp/8/3p1b2/8/1NQ1P1B1/PP2nPPP/2R2RK1 w - - 1 19 Finding Target Apple Intelligence / Personal Knowledge Graph Affected macOS Class Privacy Personalized AI What if we told you that every Mac ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, whom you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe us? Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page ( man 8 knowledgeconstructiond ), and this is all you get: man 8 knowledgeconstructiond macOS 26.6.2, build 25G83 NAME knowledgeconstructiond – A daemon that analyzes content on the device to build a general purpose knowledge graph. DESCRIPTION knowledgeconstructiond analyzes the content on this device to help build a knowledge graph representing the device and the user. It works together with intelligenceplatformd, performing some of the heavy processing tasks, to generate the knowledge graph. Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. Also, we personally ran into it in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform ; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work . I mean, if forensics folks know about this, we don't see why you should not... But we go a bit deeper. This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing). To this end, we open-source a local dashboard ( iKnow ) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac. Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: understand how attackers might exploit it. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM). We stress that this goes beyond the specific Apple personal knowledge graph, but it generally applies to any such personalized ML / assistant systems (Muse, Dot, etc.) What's in the personal knowledge graph? The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform , a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access. Likely, the most interesting is graph.db . It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity (a person, an app, an event); the object is either a plain value (a name, a handle, a date) or another entity, which is where the graph gets its edges. The predicate is the interesting part: it says what kind of relationship the system believes holds between the two. an edge, and the rows it is stored as (Me) the owner of this Mac 9100000000007919 PS500 employer CS165 employment relationship type PS45 member of Halden Labs an organization 9100000000013724 STABLE_GRAPH · THE SAME EDGE, AS THE TWO ROWS IT IS subject predicate relationshipId relationshipPredicate object 9100000000007919 PS500 4412 PS1 CS165 9100000000007919 PS500 4412 PS45 9100000000013724 every row also carries confidence, sources, sourceDuplicates and timestamp One edge of the graph (synthetic data): a person and the organization the store holds as their employer. PS500 is the id predicate.json gives employer , and its range is not an organization but a relationship type — so one edge is two rows sharing a relationshipId , one naming the kind of relationship and one pointing at the other entity. The forty-six relationship type classes in the table below exist to carry exactly that, which is what lets an edge hold a confidence of its own and be retracted later. Most of what the two daemons do is populate those predicates, and the tables kept beside them, from everything the OS will let them read. Into the graph go Contacts; Photos (faces); Calendar (titles and attendees); Family Sharing (including the age of every member); the Medical ID emergency contact in Health; events and contacts Siri Suggestions finds in Mail and Messages; people donated by apps through App Intents; and installed apps. Beside it, in tables of their own, sit who appears with whom in your photos; the communication log (who, when, which app, which direction; no content), which also pulls from your other devices; location and movement; and a long tail of device signals (screen locked, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, charging, ambient light, and a stream named ContextualUnderstanding.PhysicalSocial whose record format lists people by name, phone and email, each with a start and an end time; it reads like a log of who was physically around you, though we never saw it filled in). The first column is the id as graph.db stores it; the last says how a value gets there: copied from a source, joined from another record, derived by a rule, shipped by Apple as world knowledge, or produced by a model (in bold). Seven we could not establish, and the table says so rather than guessing. The ids and labels are Apple's; the plain-language readings are ours. How it is inferred The methods run the whole range. Most of the vocabulary is filled by plain copying (a name from Contacts, an attendee from Calendar) and rules over the copies; the interesting rows come from models: a pair of XGBoost classifiers decides who is family from 144 mostly behavioral features, two embedding models are one of ten signals the system uses to decide when two records are the same person, twelve analyzers in Photos score partner, parent, child, coworker and friend from who appears in your pictures with you, on which trips and holidays, and Apple's on-device LLM reads your messages to put a name and a relationship on a face (if Apple Intelligence is active). Whatever the method, every row lands in the graph with a confidence attached, a number between 0 and 1. The family scores live apart. Two CoreML models ship next to the ontology, EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc and EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends.mlmodelc : binary XGBoost classifiers that take 144 features and return a class and a probability over it. Their scores do not go into the triple store but into a table of their own ( entityTagging.db , one row per person, seventeen relationship columns from family to mother to coworker , recomputed every day), which is what the iKnow scorecard further down reads. Only two of those seventeen columns have a shipped model behind them; what fills the other fifteen, and how any of these probabilities would become a confidence in the graph, we could not trace. The feature names are in each model's metadata.json , in plain text. They are the clearest statement of what this system is that we have found anywhere. Sixteen of the 144: sixteen of the 144 features in metadata.json # Feature Group 5 sameLastName identity 7 photosPersonAge identity 15 nicknameContainsEmoji identity 16 sharesHomeAddress identity 18 photosAgeDifferenceCategory identity 19 iCloudFamilyMember identity 20 personOverallPopularity communication 28 personPopularityGivenSunday communication 46 personPopularityGivenNight communication 47 personPopularityGivenHome communication 57 top1PersonInteractionMechanism communication 60 photosPersonOverallPopularity photos 85 photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenMorning photos 118 photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight photos 123 photosPersonPopularityGivenHome photos 132 photosPersonPopularityGivenWeekend photos Sixteen of the 144 inputs EntityTagging_Family.mlmodelc reads, numbered by their place in its metadata.json : the six this post names, and ten that show how the rest are cut (overall, by day, by time of day, by place). EntityTagging_FamilyAndFriends reads the same 144 in the same order, and every one is a number. The groups are the schema's own three blocks: twenty on who the person is, forty on when and how you communicate with them, eighty-four on the photographs you both appear in. Two of the twenty, photosPersonAge and photosAgeDifferenceCategory , are read from Photos too. The names are Apple's; the group labels are ours. The identity group is the tidy story: same surname, same home address, an iCloud Family flag — and it is the small half. The bulk of the model is the other two: whom you message and who appears in your photographs, conditioned on the day of the week and the time of day, and then on both at once. photosPersonPosteriorProbabilityGivenSaturdayNight is a shipped feature name in a shipped classifier whose job is deciding whether someone is family. Deleting something does not delete it everywhere. The live graph forgets. Delete a contact and nothing re-derives them; the next run replaces the table wholesale. But the store keeps a second table, expired_stable_graph , beside the live one. The retracted row moves there and keeps its confidence and its sources. How long it stays there is not clear from what we could see. It seems to go after about 48 hours (the store keeps a prune watermark, and a recent snapshot of the table reached back no further than that); but on our own Mac, we could still read very old records in it. And a conclusion can outlive the evidence for it. On our Mac, the scorecard still scored two people the graph had dropped the day before, both of them known to it only from a calendar invitation. Look into your own data Is any of this sensitive? We'll leave that to you, since "sensitive" means different things to different people (though we think you have plenty to choose from here). However, the thing is, none of it lives in isolation. The sixty-one faint ones are the part nobody expects: people the store knows and has not placed, in it because they wrote to you once, or because they were on somebody else's invitation. The most important point, though, is that this is not only about you (the person using the Mac). The people around you are in it too: your family, your friends, "anyone" you have talked to through your device. None of them was asked, and the store links them to you and, through the events and groups they share, to each other. A relationship is intelligence one level above the rows it was inferred from. For instance, by correlating across our own store, we (well, an LLM working for us) could easily work out the following: That there is a child in the household, and roughly how old. The family-member types and a family circle give the household. The scorecard's child and son/daughter columns give the child's place in it. Beside it sits an age, copied from Family Sharing; and dates of birth in the store can carry the system's own word imputed , though what the system means by it is not clear to us. Which daycare the child goes to, and both of the numbers that reach it. Copied off contact cards. Note what is not there: the calendar has no school-run event, so the store holds the institution and its lines but not the hour the child is dropped off. That is still enough to call a parent from a number their phone already trusts. Where the family will be, on which days, between which hours. One calendar event, a place, two stored time slots and a title that names the family (so the guest list is in the string even where the attendee rows are empty). Which of the family will be there. The scorecard names the ones scored as family, a household entity holds them together, and a Family Sharing circle says which of them are in the same family group. And, in the same file, what is installed on the machine, down to the password manager. It is easy to see how this could be weaponized if this single point of failure for your privacy ends up in the wrong hands. We play that (hypothetical) scenario out in a second write-up . The good thing is that this knowledge is meant to stay local on your machine, protected by the Full Disk Access permission; although it can be consumed by other services (but it is not entirely clear to us how and what can be accessed). The reality is that the amount of information in this store is really something else: every time we dig into what the daemons infer, and how, a few new lines of investigation open up. Whatever you would rather no one knew about you or your family may well be in there somewhere, and we think you have the right to know whether it is. What you get instead: no documentation, no way to inspect the store and no general way to correct an inference that is wrong. So we give you two tools. The first is iKnow , a local dashboard for browsing your own graph without anything leaving your Mac (the next section walks through it). The second is for going deeper. The iKnow repository ships a manual for your own agent that tells it where the databases are and how to read them, so it can go looking for whatever you are after. (Please point a self-hosted model at it, not a cloud one.) iKnow We designed iKnow as a web dashboard implemented in the Python standard library; no npm and no CDN. It is meant to be run directly on your Mac, where the databases are stored. When executed, it binds 127.0.0.1 , locates the databases in your file system (granted the necessary permissions), opens them read-only, collects the info on the fly and represents it on a dashboard. Nothing is written and nothing is logged; values go from the stores, over loopback, into a browser tab; it can be run air-gapped if you want. We have tested it on macOS 26.6.2 and 26.7.1, and, only partially, on 27.0.1. iKnow has a dozen pages. Start here What your Mac knows. The landing page: the graph of people around you. Below it come the faces in your photos, your family, your handles, your correspondents and where you will be next. Its graph is the same household as the one at the top of this post, this time drawn by the tool's own renderer: the landing page The first screen. The white node marked (Me) is the owner of the Mac; the rest are the people, employers and group chats the store links to it, colored by what it says each one is . Orange is family, as scored. Blue is a closeness score above the cut. The faded names around the edges are people the store knows and has not placed. Nothing here is summarized that is not in the record: every node is a row, and clicking one shows you the row (which is what the graph at the top of this post does too). The graph is the overview, and an overview is easy to shrug at. The pages behind it are not. Social graph. Whom the store links to whom through shared meetings, group chats and a closeness score. Each circle opens to its members and to the evidence behind it. What it concluded Kinship scorecard. The family bindings inferred by the daemon. Its card on the landing page is cut down to the people it names: Family, as the scorecard has it Six people, six relationships, and a subtitle saying nobody typed any of it. That holds for the scores; some of what they are computed from, you did type (a relation on a contact card, an emergency contact, Family Sharing). A mother, a father and a daughter at 0.960, which is as high as these columns go; a brother, a son and a sister at 0.500. Below that is the part we find hardest to argue with. Nine separate checks (the partner column, the composite score, the household group entity, the Family Sharing token, the iCloud Family flag, top twelve-month contact, a Photos face cluster, a Contacts record, a reachable handle), and the card counts how many of them land on the same person. Eight of nine on the mother; seven on the father, and seven on Priya Sandoval, the partner, who is not in the list above: iKnow lists the relationships that roll up into another column ( mother and father into parent ), and partner rolls up into nothing. The join found the partner anyway. The card is a summary of one table, and iKnow draws the whole table too: Every person, every column Sorted by familyAndFriends , the broadest of the scores. The seven at the top each light up their own relationship and the column it rolls up into ( mother and father into parent , sister and brother into sibling , son and daughter into child ), and the partner is also a colleague. Further down are the friends and the rest of the office. Under them, almost everyone else is the same two cells: one repeated value on family and another on familyAndFriends , which is what the classifier writes when it has nothing to say. Two columns ( alumni and unknown ) are never used at all. The scores in these two shots are invented, and more generous than the real thing. On the Mac we took apart, only mother reached the top of the ladder; the few others it scored at all got one small vote on every family label at once, father and brother alike. What the fixture keeps is the table's grain: it only ever writes a handful of values (0.125, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.96), and most people sit on one default. The face index. A face cluster for everyone in your photos. Its co-occurrence graph does not use a single contact, message or calendar entry. It is built from your photographs alone: The face co-occurrence graph Two faces are linked when they appear in the same photograph, and that is the only input: 8,904 clustered faces over the 1,643 photographs that hold more than one. The labels are fragments of each cluster's local identifier, because there are no names to show. The owner is the hub. The knot on the left is the family, the group at the bottom right is work, and the two never share a frame. Each node wears its cluster's key face, read out of the photo library and blurred by iKnow's own switch for sharing the screen. Under the blur there is nobody: the fixture has no photo library, so every face is a synthetic portrait painted for it. This is the page's own honest point: the graph points at the face clusters and can name almost none of them (three of the twenty-nine, in the fixture). It does not need to. Who stands next to whom, how often, and which groups never meet is all there without a single name, and whoever knows the household can put the names back on in a second. Guessed or given. What you typed in and what the Mac worked out for itself live in the same table. A confidence score is the only thing separating them. What it recorded A year of contact. Whom you talked to, when, and not a word of message text (and it does not need any to tell when you are asleep). Its card on the landing page is the one that gets the reaction, and it contains no inference at all. A year of who you talked to A year of contact, per person, split incoming and outgoing, with call counts and a last-seen date, across five messaging apps — and, exactly as the subtitle says, not one word of message text. None of this is content. It is all metadata, and it is enough. The last line is the one to read twice: the hours it can read as sleep. iKnow draws that line too, from the same log folded onto a single week: Weekday against hour of day Every cell counts the messages and calls that fell in one hour of one weekday, over the year. The working week is in there, and so are the evenings and the late weekend mornings; and so is the pale band from one to seven, every night. Nobody stored a sleep schedule. The quietest six-hour stretch falls out of the timestamps for free. That is the general shape of this store: almost nothing in it had to be collected, because almost everything in it is a consequence of something that was. The calendar. The one layer that knows where you will be: the hour, the room, the attendees and the dial-in. What you withdrew. Withdrawing a fact does not remove it. The row moves to an expired table and keeps its confidence and provenance. The machinery The store. The file itself: what it models, and two real rows expanded into everything they touch. Device fingerprint. Every app installed on the Mac is written down in plain text, next to a token that is an unsalted SHA-256 of that same app identifier, so the page recomputes it in your browser and you can watch it match. Who else reads it. The graph is the first copy, not the only one. This page maps the views that subscribe to it, the databases they publish into, the tables that repeat the same facts, the streams coming in from hardware paired with the Mac, and the machinery that is set up but has not run yet. A note on macOS 27. macOS 27 was released on September 14, 2026. After the upgrade to 27.0.1, the graph withdrew most of the rows it had built from Contacts, Calendar, Siri Suggestions, Family Sharing and the app catalog, and rebuilt them over the following day. Some pages of iKnow may not work fully on macOS 27 yet. title: Humans will never again create a project quite like Wikipedia
Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2
body_text:
New PwnEscape: Guest-to-host escape through the Linux kernel Read the research → × Product Pricing Research Company Contact Start a Pentest Back Firecracker VM Escape: PwnEscape Part 2. PWN Research, Paulos Yibelo · 19 m 19 min read Firecracker is supposed to keep untrusted code inside a microVM. We escaped it and achieved code execution as root on the host. We found how it saved registers, changed where it would resume, and made it execute a call of our choosing when it returned from KVM. The guest then restored the temporary stack changes. Firecracker kept running, and the VM remained accessible over SSH. PwnEscape Part 1 introduced the host memory primitive behind this work. Here we follow the next part of the chain: using that access to find Firecracker in memory and take over a live thread from inside the guest. This is a continuation to show CVE-2026-99999 on a Firecracker setup. 00 / Choosing where to take control A Firecracker microVM has a process on the host that manages it. Each virtual CPU, or vCPU, has a thread in that process. The thread enters KVM to run the guest and returns to Firecracker when an event needs handling in userspace. Firecracker documents this arrangement in its architecture overview . firecracker-host-integration-dbdde36ef234 The call that runs the virtual CPU looks like this: ioctl(vcpu_fd, KVM_RUN, 0 ); While the thread is in that system call, the host kernel holds its saved userspace registers in a structure called pt_regs . These registers describe the Firecracker thread: its instruction pointer says where execution should resume, and its stack pointer says which userspace stack it should use. That made the return from KVM_RUN an attractive target. If we could locate and modify the saved frame, we could choose the code Firecracker executed when the thread returned to userspace. A guest operation that caused such a return would provide the trigger. We already had access to selected host physical memory through a guest mapping. To use it, we needed to identify the Firecracker process, find code we could call in that process, and locate the register frame belonging to its active vCPU thread. The starting point was a page of memory we controlled inside the guest. 01-guest-to-vmm-chain-5c0fbee0cb07 Figure 1. The guest identifies its Firecracker process, finds the saved registers for a vCPU thread, and redirects the thread when it returns from KVM. 01 / Finding our guest page on the host The guest and host use different physical address spaces. A page has a guest physical address, or GPA, inside the VM and a host physical address, or HPA, in the machine backing it. On the target, Extended Page Tables (EPT) provide the translation between them. We placed a recognizable byte pattern, a nonce, in a guest page. The first resolver took that page's known GPA and its contents as inputs. Together, they gave us an address to translate and a way to check whether the translation reached our page. The resolver searched the host physical ranges covered by the memory primitive for candidate EPT roots. An EPT root is the starting point of the translation tables. For each candidate, the resolver followed the entries selected by the guest address until it reached a physical page, then checked that page for the nonce. The snippets below are explanatory pseudocode with descriptive helper names. They show the data passed between stages and the checks used to connect them. for root in candidate_ept_roots: page_hpa = walk_ept(root, guest_gpa) if page_hpa is invalid: continue contents = read_host(page_hpa, length(nonce)) if contents == nonce: candidates.append((root, page_hpa)) The nonce check connected a proposed translation to memory we controlled. The broader search produced two candidates; validation of the nested page tables reduced them to one EPT root. Walking that root gave us the host physical address of our guest page. We called this result guest_page_hpa and passed it to the next resolver. We now had a recognizable object in host memory. The next task was finding the host process that mapped it. 02 / Finding the Firecracker process Firecracker maps memory used by the guest into its own address space. That mapping gave us a way to work backward from the guest page to the process. Host processes use page tables to translate their virtual addresses into physical memory. The top level is called the page global directory, or PGD. Recovering the appropriate PGD would let us translate addresses inside Firecracker and read its code and stack through the memory primitive. Our reverse mapper searched the native host page tables for a mapping of guest_page_hpa . A normal page table walk starts with a virtual address and produces a physical address. Here, we looked for a mapping to a physical page we already knew, then recovered the virtual address and page table root associated with it. The check runs in both directions: for mapping in reverse_map_host_page_tables(guest_page_hpa): pgd = mapping.root guest_page_va = mapping.virtual_address resolved_hpa = walk_host_page_tables(pgd, guest_page_va) if resolved_hpa != guest_page_hpa: continue if read_host(resolved_hpa, length(nonce)) != nonce: continue process_candidates.append((pgd, guest_page_va)) This connected the host process's virtual mapping to the physical page found through EPT. The reverse mapper returned one validated address space. We retained its root as host_pgd and used it to inspect the process. The next resolver looked for the Firecracker executable in those mappings. It identified an ELF image and checked a known byte sequence in Firecracker's write(2) wrapper. That connected the recovered address space to the binary we were targeting. ASLR changes where an executable is loaded. The difference between an address in the ELF image and its corresponding runtime address is the load bias. Once the mapper had identified the image, it could recover that bias and use it to locate the code required by the exploit: runtime_code_address = load_bias + code_address_in_elf The mapper returned the load bias as firecracker_base . With that value and host_pgd , we could locate code in the running process, translate its virtual address to host physical memory, and compare the bytes there with the expected binary. We checked three locations: the write(2) wrapper that would produce our proof, the continuation after the KVM ioctl, and a short xor eax,eax; ret sequence needed to return cleanly. Their purposes become relevant when we construct the return path below. At this point, the guest could inspect the Firecracker image and its private mappings. We still needed the saved registers of the thread currently running our VM. 02-address-resolution-0e47fd8bf102 Figure 2. The nonce identifies the guest page in host memory. Its mapping leads to a host page table root, which lets the next resolver locate and validate the Firecracker image. 03 / Locating the live vCPU frame The frame finder took host_pgd and firecracker_base from the preceding stages. It used them to recognize the host thread's saved state. The most useful clue was the return address. A vCPU thread in KVM_RUN should have a saved instruction pointer at the corresponding ioctl continuation in Firecracker. We could calculate that address from the validated binary and its load bias. We then searched host memory for a pt_regs frame consistent with that call. An address match alone would also pick up stale stack contents, so the candidate had to satisfy several related checks: Saved state What we checked System call The syscall identity and in-progress state matched an active ioctl. Request argument The ioctl request was KVM_RUN . File descriptor The descriptor fell within the helper's expected range. Instruction pointer It matched the validated Firecracker ioctl continuation. Stack pointer It translated through the recovered host PGD. Segment selectors and flags They described a valid return to userspace. Caller return address It fell inside the validated Firecracker text mapping. The stack check tied the frame to the same address space we had recovered from the guest page. The instruction and caller addresses tied it to the Firecracker image. The syscall fields tied it to the operation running the vCPU. The search left one candidate. Its location was stored as frame_hpa , the host physical address of the saved register frame. We passed it, the PGD, and the load bias to the final helper. Before changing memory, the helper repeated the code signature, frame, and stack checks. This ensured that the active stage used the same process state the resolvers had identified. The subsequent execution and recovery checks would establish that the selected frame was live. 03-live-kvm-run-frame-ddb3ad26cf50 Figure 3. The candidate register frame must agree with the KVM ioctl, the recovered process page tables, and the validated Firecracker code. 04 / Redirecting the return from KVM We chose a simple payload: make the Firecracker process write a recognizable string to its own stderr. This would give the host runner an observable result from the process we had taken over. The string was N8V23M2
 , seven characters followed by a newline. It occupies eight bytes and fits in one stack word. The call we wanted Firecracker to execute was: write( 2 , "N8V23M2
" , 8 ); Here 2 is Firecracker's stderr file descriptor. The buffer pointer must refer to the string in Firecracker's address space, so we stored the string on its private userspace stack. We saved three stack words before modifying them. One held the string; the other two held the return addresses for the temporary call sequence. We then changed the saved register frame to supply the wrapper address, its arguments, and a stack pointer for that sequence: RIP = address of Firecracker's write wrapper RDI = 2 RSI = virtual address of the marker on Firecracker's stack RDX = 8 RSP = virtual address of the temporary return sequence Returning from write also needed care. A successful write of eight bytes returns 8 , while a successful KVM_RUN call returns zero . We placed the address of xor eax,eax; ret first in the return sequence. It clears the return value before the second address brings execution back to Firecracker's original ioctl continuation. The resulting control flow was: KVM_RUN returns to userspace -> Firecracker's write wrapper emits the marker -> xor eax,eax; ret sets the return value to zero -> execution resumes at the original ioctl continuation With the stack and saved registers prepared, the guest wrote one byte to its serial port. That operation caused the vCPU thread to return from KVM_RUN . The kernel restored the modified registers, and Firecracker entered the write wrapper with our arguments. The wrapper emitted the marker, the return sequence cleared eax , and the thread rejoined its original execution path. After control returned to the guest, the helper restored all three stack words. 04-reversible-control-flow-10ae6af41746 Figure 4. The saved register frame enters the write wrapper. Two return addresses lead through the return-value adjustment and back into the original Firecracker path. 05 / Checking execution and recovery The host runner captured Firecracker's stderr separately from the guest. The complete output was: N8V23M2 The capture contained exactly eight bytes, including the final newline. Firecracker was still running, guest SSH was responsive, and the helper had restored the three temporary stack words. We checked recovery with a fresh pass that made no memory changes. It was given the same frame address and repeated the register, code, and stack checks after the trigger. The checks passed, and it found no stale marker in the temporary stack location. These observations answered three different questions. The guest log recorded the trigger and restoration. The host capture showed that Firecracker executed the selected operation. The final validation checked the state after execution. Check Recorded result Firecracker stderr One copy of the marker, eight bytes in total Firecracker process PID 2936 , alive after the trigger Guest health SSH responsive; uptime 1615.72 seconds Temporary stack state All three original words restored Executable text and shared libraries Unmodified Host kernel errors after the trigger None observed Validation after restoration The supplied frame address and surrounding invariants passed 05-proof-receipt-6e8ad89bf50c Figure 5. The guest log, Firecracker stderr capture, and final validation record the trigger, host execution, and restored state. 06 / Root execution on the host By the time the marker appeared, the guest had selected the host thread's instruction pointer, function arguments, stack data, and return path. Firecracker executed the call using its own privileges. The target was Firecracker v1.16.1 on x86-64, with host kernel 7.0.0-1011-aws and guest kernel 6.18.44+ . We launched Firecracker directly as root under systemd-run and pinned it with taskset . Consequently, the controlled call executed as root on the host. The existing write wrapper gave us a compact proof of that control. Extending it to other calls would require choosing code and arguments compatible with the process's mappings and syscall policy. The configuration used here had no jailer. Firecracker's production containment includes dropping privileges and restricting the process through namespaces and seccomp. A deployment using those controls requires a separate assessment of the privileges and resources available after compromising its VMM. The address discovery is what lets the exploit follow the running instance. The EPT resolver connects a guest page to host memory; the reverse mapper recovers the host address space; the image mapper locates Firecracker under ASLR; and the frame finder identifies the vCPU's saved state. Adapting the final stage to another build requires validating that binary's code signatures and return path. The guest had used access to host memory to take over the thread running the VM itself. A serial write supplied the trigger, and the next userspace operation belonged to us. Captured resolver values and artifacts The following values come from the preserved execution record. The methods above use symbolic names so that the role of each value is clear; this table connects those names to the recorded addresses. Value Recorded address Where it enters the chain guest_gpa 0x08f03000 The guest physical address of the nonce page, supplied to the first resolver guest_page_hpa 0x165610000 The host address of that page, found by the EPT resolver host_pgd 0x14afc2000 The host page table root recovered by the reverse mapper firecracker_base 0x7298c2400000 The Firecracker load bias recovered by the image mapper frame_hpa 0x13a5bff48 The saved register frame selected for the active stage The records use run ID eventpath-v23-0907self02 and boot ID 2b3cd5ac-2311-427f-a50a-6a79ecb8daa7 . These identifiers connect the resolver records, host capture, and validation after restoration. The earlier memory provider also received host-selected task and canary page frame numbers as independent validation overlays after constructing the memory aperture. Those addresses were not consumed by the EPT resolver, reverse mapper, Firecracker mapper, frame finder, or final marker helper. The release bundle contains the final helper source, JSONL resolver records, host capture, recovery manifest, four preserved read-only resolver binaries with provenance, and SHA-256 manifests. The final helper accepts the PGD, load bias, and frame HPA produced by the resolvers. Its checks cover the run identifier, address ranges, code signatures, saved registers, and stack geometry; its dry-run mode performs validation without writing memory. body_text: Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why: no “Starting” screen and 70% less RAM, even with two accounts signed in Facebook Mail RSS Twitter Youtube Windows 11 Windows 10 Windows 10 PC Apps & Games Privacy Policy Contact Us About us Select Theme: System Light Dim Dark Search Sign in Welcome! Windows 10 has 11 months left, and… Microsoft killed Windows 10 to push Windows 11, but Windows sales… Microsoft extended Windows 10, but Nvidia just made the extension meaningless… Microsoft is limiting Microsoft 365 & OneDrive on Windows 10 to… Privacy Policy Contact Us About us Select Theme: System Light Dim Dark Trending: Remove Recall AI New Start menu Windows 11 25H2 New Windows 11 ISO Windows 11 24H2 Windows 11 AI requirements Restore WordPad Home Windows 11 Windows 11 Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why: no “Starting” screen and 70% less RAM, even with two accounts signed in By Abhijith M B - November 6, 2026 0 Discord’s current Electron client and its new Rust client launching side by side on two Lenovo ThinkPads running Windows 11 Discord’s new Rust client had its friends list loaded before the current Electron app could get past its loading screen, in a 15-second clip that we found on the X account of Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy . The video had 2.3 million views at the time of writing, and Discord employees have confirmed that both apps were launched from a cold start. Vishnevskiy also revealed that the 290.2MB RAM usage on the Task Manager of the new client, which shows up as Discord Phoenix, came with two accounts signed in at once, which justifies the already efficient RAM usage. Discord Rust for Windows 11 Discord’s Rust client opens before the Electron app finishes loading “The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time,” Vishnevskiy wrote on X , and Discord’s official account also shared the clip with the current client on the left and the Rust rebuild on the right. https://www.windowslatest.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Electron-Discord-vs-Rust-Discord-where-the-new-client-opens-must-faster-than-the-old-one.mp4 We went through the video frame by frame. What’s impressive is that the current client is opened first and shows a blank dark window for about three seconds, followed by a tip that reads “In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app.” Funnily enough, the Electron app still carries a browser engine today. The new client is double-clicked roughly a second and a half later, yet its window fades in within a second. When the old app reaches its interface, about five seconds after launch, the Rust version already has the friends list loaded, while the Electron client briefly says “There are no friends online at this time.” Discord Windows app. Credit: Windows Latest Of course, people on X asked if the new app simply popped out of the system tray. “Both are cold starts, it’s really that fast. We’ve been using it internally now for a while and the first time I tried it I thought I’d forgot to close it when I opened it fresh,” replied Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord. Travis, who works on socials and community at Discord and filmed the clip, added that a tray launch would mean “the friends list would have already been loaded!” Vishnevskiy thanked him for “finding these janky old laptops,” which are ThinkPads with a Copilot key, so 2024 or newer, which I wouldn’t dare call janky or old. They’re beautiful machines! The new Discord app skips the “Starting” screen and updates in the background As you’d already know, the current app usually checks for updates and shows a “Starting” screen when you open it, which one person on X said “takes like 5-10s every time.” Asked why the new client skips it, coral said, “It bootstraps so fast + is a new architecture so we don’t need that modal at all. We auto-update in the background.” Discord starting animation. Credit: Windows Latest Discord isn’t handing updates to the Microsoft Store or Windows’ Update Orchestration Platform either, as Coral said “We do not at this moment” when asked. Discord’s Rust client uses about 70% less RAM with two accounts signed in When one reply called 290MB “still vile” for a chat app, Vishnevskiy said, “Those 4k avatar decorations gotta render somewhere ;) but joking aside this client is actually running 2 accounts concurrently which is supported in new client.” Today’s Account Switcher lets you add up to five accounts and swap between them. Asked if the new client could keep work and personal accounts running “without needing to tear down the client in between,” Vishnevskiy replied “Yup.” Again, impressive and exciting. Discord idle RAM usage. Credit: Windows Latest For comparison, a Discord employee said in December 2025 that normal usage is under 1GB, while the company tested auto-restarting the app at 4GB . So, 290.2MB is about 70% below the 1GB mark, and on our PCs, the Electron app usually idles at 1-2GB. To be clear, it’s a snapshot from an early build, and Discord hasn’t published a like-for-like benchmark of both clients, but we’ll be doing that test when we get hands-on with the Rust version. Discord did try to fix Electron from the inside. Its September patch notes say the Electron 42 upgrade cut median CPU usage by about 17%, but “at the cost of a smaller regression to p50 memory usage (~4%).” Even the Game Mode toggle it tested later doesn’t mention RAM. Discord is replacing Electron with GPUI, not Tauri Electron inherits its multi-process architecture from Chromium , so every Electron app comes with its own browser engine, with a main process and a renderer process for each window. Tauri, which many guessed Discord would pick, uses Rust for app logic but builds the interface in HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside the system’s webview , which is WebView2 on Windows. Discord went with GPUI , “A fast, hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework for Rust” from the makers of the Zed code editor. GPUI draws the interface on the GPU without any HTML, and Rust, which Discord has used since 2018, manages memory without a garbage collector. Technology What it is Role in Discord Rust Programming language New client and shared app code GPUI Rust UI framework from Zed Draws the new desktop app Electron Chromium and Node.js runtime Current desktop app, being removed Tauri Rust framework using the system webview Not used React Native Mobile app framework Current mobile apps, being removed   Why not WinUI, you ask? (At least, I thought of it). Discord hasn’t mentioned it, and it was unlikely to, as Microsoft’s native framework only runs on Windows, while GPUI already powers Zed on Windows, macOS and Linux. Discord has its own patches on top of GPUI, and Vishnevskiy said “we will see what we can upstream if relevant to the community.” Web tech stays where it makes sense, as YouTube embeds and Activities will use the system webview. “We use the native webview similar to Tauri,” Vishnevskiy said about Activities. Discord’s mobile apps drop React Native, and the web app moves to WebAssembly Phones keep native interfaces but will share app code with desktop through Rust. On React Native, Vishnevskiy explained, “Since the beginning the iOS app started as React native, Android was ported to React Native couple years ago to achieve parity as it was always lagging in features.” The browser version will keep rendering HTML, but “logic will be WASM instead of JS.” WebAssembly (WASM) lets code written in languages like Rust run inside a browser, so the web app can share the Rust code too. As for the look, whether you like it or not, “The app looks and works identically to the current one,” Vishnevskiy said. Discord’s Rust client goes into private testing soon If you can’t to try it out, Discord marketing director Ryan K. Rigney said, “Going into private testing soon. Gonna take our time to make sure it’s stable and secure first. Won’t be long, tho.” I would rather wait for them to iron out any bugs. Mark Smith , Discord’s VP of Engineering, added that “accessibility and security are just as important to us as performance,” and Coral confirmed the new client keeps your login token in the system keyring, which is Credential Manager on Windows 10 and 11. Of course, Discord is not just doing all this work for Windows. When asked if it works on Linux, Rigney replied, “Yes,” and Coral said, “a lot of people run Mac internally!” Discord hasn’t announced a public release date yet. Discord just made WhatsApp and Teams look worse on Windows 11 Electron made it easier for Discord to ship one desktop app on Windows, macOS, and Linux for a decade. But Discord has now shown that a chat app with millions of users can drop the bundled browser without a redesign. WhatsApp, Teams and Discord combined using 1.5GB RAM while being idle. Credit: Windows Latest As for the owners of the biggest messaging platforms for regular users and enterprises, Meta and Microsoft are running out of excuses. WhatsApp went from a native app that idled under 100MB to a WebView2 wrapper using up to 1.2GB , and I uninstalled it. Microsoft Teams also uses WebView2, took up 963MB doing nothing in our tests , and it doesn’t look like Redmond cares enough to go native, despite pushing WinUI. Ironically, AI got us here. Data centers soaked up DRAM supply, prices shot up, and Windows chief Pavan Davuluri now says “memory is top of mind for us right now in the industry” as Microsoft trims Windows 11’s RAM usage . Apps that kept asking for more RAM are finally going on a diet, and we’ve come full circle. Are you waiting to try the Rust-based Discord when it rolls out? Support original journalism. Boston Bay Area South Florida San Diego Connecticut tv Today Nightly News Meet the Press Dateline Featured NBC News Now Nightly Films Stay Tuned Special Features Newsletters Podcasts Listen Now Business in America More From NBC NBC.COM NBCU Academy Peacock NEXT STEPS FOR VETS NBC News Site Map Help Follow NBC News news Alerts There are no new alerts at this time Search Search Facebook Twitter Email SMS Blue Sky Whatsapp Print Reddit Flipboard Pinterest Linkedin Latest Stories Politics U.S. News World Sports Business Health Selected Tipline Tech News Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production after years of poor sales in few markets Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Tesla to wind down production of Cybertruck 01:31 Get more news Live on Share Add NBC News to Google Nov. 6, 2026, 8:36 AM EST / Source : Reuters By Reuters Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, CEO Elon Musk said on Friday, after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks that ultimately only sold in just a handful of markets because of its heavy, angular design. Musk said in an X post the production wind-down would enable the automaker to accommodate increased output of its newly launched Cybercab model, which the billionaire has made central to Tesla's robotaxi ambitions. While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would be moved to another facility or phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the model's specialized components. In response to a user on X, Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era." Tesla did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The US EV maker only began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023. According to Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. Before the pickup truck launched, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units. "It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer. "Every rational auto guy would say the same." "It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves." Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Musk. Its angular design was mocked by pickup truck purists and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe. The unveiling event itself was marred when Musk tried to prove that its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them - only to leave massive cracks in two of them. During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future." But the vehicle has struggled to meet those expectations. Automotive analyst Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market. "All of them lost the competition because electric pick ups aren't popular in the US," Munoz said. But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe where EVs are more popular. Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact. "Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," former Aston Martin CEO Palmer said. The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker. Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis. After years of delays to Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September. However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards. "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.
